abacot.c: A BACOT, the Cap os State, used in old time by our English swings, wrought up in the Figure of two Crowns.

abactors.c: ABACTORS, the same with Abigei, such as steal and drive away whole Flocks of Cattle, or the greatest part of any Herd or Flock; in which the Lawyers distinguish them from Sures, who only steal a Sheep or two, &c.

abacus.c: ABACUS, sometimes signifies the A, B, C. sometimes a Table of Numbers for casting up Accounts, which was anciently of Brass, and called then. The Table of Pythagoras. It signifies also sometimes the Numeral Figures, which used to be drawn on a Table covered with small Sand Or Dust, as Persius hints in these Verses, Nec qui Abaco numeros scela in pu lucre notas Scit risijfe vafer -.

ABACUS, in Architecture, is the four square Table that makes the Capital on the Top of a Column, especially those of the Corinthian Order, and is a Drip or Corona to the Capital. It supports the neither Face of the Architrave and whole Trabeation. In the Corinthian and Comfojitt Orders, the Corners of it are called, the Horns - the middle part the Sweep, and the Curvature, the Arch ; which commonly has a Rose carved in the middle.

abaft.c: ABAFT, or Aft, aSea-term, signifying always those Parts which are towards the Stern of the Ship : So they say, Such a Mast hangs Aft or Abaft, that is, towards the Stern. And because the Master’s or Captain’s Cabbin is usually in the hinder part of the Ship under the Quarter Deck, tis a common Complement to a Person come on Board a Ship, Sir, will you please towall^Aft.

abalienation.c: ABALIENATION, a 1 Term in the old t{pman *^w, signifying a simple Sale of the Goods ol one Citizen to another: These Goods were called, Res rn<, ncupii t or mancipii ; and were Estates either lfc Slaves or Cattle, and sometimes Land of Inheritance ; but they must be in Italy.

abaptiston.c: ABAPTISTON, or Anabaptiston , an Instrument used by Surgeons, the same with Modiolus, which see.

abate.c: ABATE, Abatement , signifies in Law the taking Possession of Land by a Person that hath no right ro ir, after the Death of the Ancestor, and before the Entry of the right Heir. Also to Abate a Writ, signifies to destroy it for a time, thro’ want of good Ground, or other defect. So to Abate a Nusance, is to destroy it, &c.

abatementofhonour.c:
ABATEMENT of Honour, in Heraldry, is an Accidental Mark annexed to a Coat of Arms, whereby its Dignity is abased by reason of som* dilhonourable Quality or Srain in the Bearer, and ’tis either by adding a Mark, of Diminution ; or by Reversion of the whole Escutcheon. The Mark> of Diminution are , IA Dess , which is a Square born in the middle of the Field , thus ; and belongs to one that hath revoked his Challenge, or eaten his Words. 2. A Point Dexter parted Tenn: due to him that is a Braggadocio, or boasts of more than he did, or can do. 3 . A Point in Point Sanguine, thus ; due to him that is Lazy and Slsathful in the Wars. 4 . A Point Champain Tcnn : which is due to him that kills his Prisoner after Quarter demanded and his Commander's leave to give it f born thus. B A Plain

AB D ABO 5, A Plain Point Sanguine, born thus ; due to one that is a Lyar, and tells false Stories to his Soveraign. 6. A Goar Sinijlcr Tcnn , bom thus j and is due to him that is proved a Coward : But a Goar Dexter is not an Abatement. 7. A Gusset Sanguine, born thus ; where are two Gussets one on each side. The Gusset is an Abatement proper for an Effeminate , Lascivious Man ; and is then born on the Rightside ; but if he be givsn to too much Wine, the Gusset is on the Lcft-side ; if to both, he should bear two Gussets , as in this Example. Reversion is two-fold, 1. When a Man bears in his own Escutcheon another Reversed, as thus; which is due to a Rude and Uncivil Treater of Maid or Widow j or as some say, for Deflowring her only; and also, for one that runneth a way from his sovereign’s Banner. Z. When a Man’s own Escutcheon is entirely Reversed, which is due to a Traitor. N. B. These Abatements are never charged with any thing; are always born single, and their Colour is never of Metal, but always either Murrey or Tawncy.

abator.c: ABATOR, (in the (Joinmon Law J is he that abateth, that is, intrude th into a House or Land void by the Death of the former Possessor, and not yet entred, or taken up by his Heir.

abbrochment.c: ABBROCHMENT.is the forestalling of a Market or Fair, by buying up the Wares before they are exposed to sale in such Market or Fair, and then vending them again by Retail.

abbuttalls.c: ABBUTTALLS, are the Buttings and Bouncings of Lands any way, shewing how they lie in respect to other places.

abdication.c: ABDICATION, a Term of the Roman Law, signifying several things; as the Abandoning of a Son, when he was expelled his Father’s House and refused to be owned as his Child. Abdicare MagiJlratum, or fe Magiflratu, was to abandon or lay down the Office of a Magistrate. We meet there also with Abdicare fe Jlatu suo ; which signifies, a Man’s renouncing his Condition, to become a Slave, and to be degraded from the Privileges of , a Roman Citizen.

abdicere.c: ABDICERE, signifies to debar a Man from his Demands or not to allow them : Thus Abdicere vindicias was in the Rpman Law not to allow a Man the Possession of a Thing in conrroversic ; as Addiccre vindicias is the very contrary. Tho’ the word Abdication signifies strictly an . actual and voluntary Renouncing, yet in a larger Sense, at Common-Law, it may be properly used wbcVe there is only an Implicit Renunciation ; ‘as when a Person does such Actions which are inconsistent with the nature of his Trust,, he does in consequence renounce it; and this was the late famous Case of a certain Prince, where this known and ancient Cotnmon-Law Term was revived ; tho’ indeed ’ris more generally used amongst the Civilians.

abdomen.c: ABDOMEN,the lowermost of the three Venters in an Humane Body; properly th c Lower Belly It contains in its Region the Stomach, Gutts, Liver, Spleen, Bladder, Ose. within it is covered with a Membrane called the Peritoneum. The lower part of it is called the Hypogailrium. The foremost part is divided into the Epigastrium , the Right and Left Hypochondria's, and the Navel. ’Tis bounded above by the Cartilago Ensifortnis and the Diaphragm, sideways by the short or lower Ribs, and behind by the Vertebresof the Loins, the Bones of the Coxendix , Pubts, and Os sacrum. It harsh ten Muscles which both cover it and serve to excrete the Rtcej and Urine, and to expel the Foetus in Women: You will find them under their proper Names. ABDUCT OR Indicts, is a Muscle of the ForcFinger, which is not to be seen till the Abdudor Pollicis is raised ; by some it is reckoned amongst the Int crossci ; it arises lie Illy from the Os Metacarpi that sustains the FoYe-tinger, and descending ever the first Internode of the laid Finger becomes Tendinous, joiivng with the Tendon of one of the Lumbrical Mule es, and is inserted with it together with the Tendon of the former Mulce. Its Name intimates its use, in drawing the Forefinger from the rest.

abductoroculi.c: ABDUCTOR Ocuti, a Muscle of the Eye, so called from its Action in retracting or drawing off the Eye from the No set is also called Indignabundus , because it is made use of in scornful Resentments.

abductorminimidigiti.c:
ABDUCTOR minimi digiti, is a Muscle which appears in some Bodies divided into two or three Muscles, having each a differing Series of Fibres j the first of which seems to be a Flexor primi Internedii minimi Digiti ; the second an Abduclor of j the same ; the third Abdudor Secundi & Tertii I Internodii ; but this Division .s not constant. It arises fleshy, first, from the Ligamcntum Transversal, and fourth Bone of the Carpus ; Secondly, from the third Bone of the Carpus ; and then, Thirdly, from the superior parts of the subjacent Os Metacarpi : The two first continue fleshy to their Insertions; the former terminating ac the superior part of the first Bone of the Little finger forwards; the latter ending at the same part of the said Bone laterally; ‘the Third becoming Tendinous like the Interosfei, is inserted like them with the Tendon of the Extensor Minimi Digiti at the superior part of the third Bone of the Little-Finger. Its use is to draw the Li;- tle-Fingcr from the others, j ABD U CTOR Poilicts, is a Muscle of the Thumb, ! which arises broad and fleshy from the internal part of the Ligamcntum Tranjver/ale Carpi , whence descending it lessens it self, and becomes Tendinous ac its Implantation to the superior and external part of the second Bone of the Thumb laterally. This draws the Thumb from che Fingers, from whence it derives its Name. ABDUCTOR Pollicis Pcdis, is a Muscle which ariseth fleshy from the OsCalcis internally and laterally, in half its progress becoming Tendinous, it joins with another fleshy beginning, springing from

AB L A B S from the Os Cunoforme m.ijus that sustains the Os Eletaiarji of the Great Toe; both which making one Tendon are inserted to the external part of the Os Sefamoides of the Great Toe laterally. This pulls the Great Toe from the rest. ABDUC1 OR. Minimi Digits Pcdis, is a Mqlclc which arileth outwardly Tendinous, but inwardly Fleshy, from the external part of the Os C ale is, becoming Tendinous in half its progress on the outside of the Foot; it joins with the other fleshy part of this Muscle arising fleshy from the outside of the Os Metatarsi of the Little Toe, and making one Tendon at its Insertion to the upper part of the first Bone of the Little Toe externally and laterally. Its use is to draw off the Little Toe from the rest.

abductores.c: ABDUCTORES, in the general arc the same With Abducent Muscles.

abducentmuscles.c: ABDUCENT Muscles , are universally those which serve to open or pull back divers parts of the Body, as the Arms, Legs, Eyes, Nostrils, Lips,Ac. 1ht.fe are called also Abduclois. Their Opposites are usually called Adductors or Adducent Muscles ABETTORS, is a Common Law Term, and Agni ties thole that without cause procure others to sue out false Appeals of Murder or Felony against Men, in order to render them infamous.

abettorsinmurder.c: ABETTORS in Murder,are those which advise or pr court a Murder to be committed . in the same Sense there are Abettors in Felony and 1 reason ; in the last of which they are all Principals, there being no Accessories in Treason.

abolition.c: ABEL1TION, the Licence given to a Criminal Accuser, to desist from further Prosecution.

abeyance.c: ABEYANCE, in Law signifies a Thing’s being «w PoJJ'e only and not in Ailu: Thus suppose a Leale made to A. for Term of Life, and the Remainder to the right Heir of B. who is living at the time of the Grant ; in this cafe, tho’ the Remainder pass presently from the Grantor, yet h vests not prelcutly, or takes hold in the Grantee, that is, the Heirs of B. but is Indeterminate, in Potentia, in Nubibus , in Abeyance, vi^. in consideration of Law : So when the Parson of a Church dies, and the Church is void, the Fee is M Abeyance, because it is not determined who shall succeed him. ABlSHERlSlNG, and in some Copies, Mijher ‘Jing, is (in Common-Law ) being acquitted of Anierceameuts, before whomsoever, of Transgression prov'd.

abiuration.c: ABJURATION, formerly was an Oath which a Person who had committed Felony, and who, to a void the Law, had betaken himself to Sanctuar y> took to depart the Kingdom for ever: It Was a Law enabled by Edward the ConfeJJbs, but is since changed by the Statutes, ai H. 8. c. a. 22. II. 8. c. tq. 3a. I-I. 8. c. I a. But the Sense of the word Abjurare originally, in the Roman Language, as it is used by Cicero and other good Writers of that Age, was, To deny a thing upon Oath to deny that a Man had promi/cd, commit- *cd, detained, or did owe any thing upon his Oath, Ihus with him Abjurare Creditum was to forswear a Debt, or to deny on Oath that he ow’d the Debt.

ablactation.c: ABLACTATION, the weaning of a Child that Kith sucked its full time. Also a kind of Grafting, when the Cyon remains on its own Stock, and the Stock you g ra st st 0 n, together, till such time *s they are surely incorporated $ then the Cyon is cut from its own, and lives only by the other Stock. ABLAQUEATlON, a laying open or baring the bottom of the Trunk and Roots of Trees, that so being exposed to the Air, the Sun, and the Rains, they may the better frucstisy, or bear Fruit the ensuing Year. ABLATIVE C<i/c, is the last of the six Cafes of Nouns and Participles in Grammar, and is so called because it usually takes away one thing from another. ’Tis called also the Latin Caje, because almost peculiar to the Latin Tongue, and is usually connected with some Prepositions which serve to determine it.

ablution.c: ABLUTION, the Preparation of a Medicine in any Liquor, to cleanse it from its Impurities.

abluentmedicines.c: ABLUENT Medicines are the same with Abstergent ; which see.

abnodation.c: ABNODATION, in Agriculture, signifies the Pruning of Trees and cutting off Knots and Knobs. ABOLlllON, inMetaphyiicks, is an utter destruction of any Being.

abolfiionofalaw.c: ABOLFI ION of a Law, is the perfect repealing ir, or the entire taking of it away, so that it shall never have force again.

abomasus.c: ABOMASUS, one of the Stomachs of Ruminant Animals, or such as chew the Cud ; of which are reckoned four, the Venter, steticuljun, Omajus, and Abomajus.

aborigines.c: ABORIGINES, are such Nations as the Italians, who pretended Antiently to be without Original or Derivation from any other Nation or People.

abortion.c: ABORTION, the bringing forth of a Child (or Eœtus) before its due time.

abortive.c: ABORTIVE, is spoken of a Foetus brought forth before its time : Hence also ’tis an Epithet given to any Design or Purpose that milcarrics.

abrenunciation.c: ABRENUNCIATION, is a renouncing or forsaking of any thing entirely.

abreviations.c: ABREVIATIONS, are Contractions in writing or otherwise, whereby any thing that is written or spoken is contained in or takes up much less Room than it would do if written or delivered at large. ABRlC,with some Chymists the lame withSulph. ABRIDGMENT of a Plaint in Common-La w, is, when one part of the Plaintiff’s Demand is left out, and it is pray’d, that the Defendant may answer to the other.

abrogate.c: ABROGATE, signifies to disannul or repeal: as to Abrogate a Law. is, to lay it aside or to repeal it. So that the

abrogationofalaw.c: ABROGATION of a Law is the Repealing it. or taking it quite away.

abscessk.c: ABSCESSK,anExulccrationarisinginany part of the Body after a Crisis : The lame with Apojlema.

absciss.c:
ABSCISSÆ, in a Gonick Section, or other Curvilineal Figure, are the Parts of the Axis, cut off by thcOrdinates, and accounted downwards from the Vertex of the Section. Thus Vr or VR are the Abfciste in this Figure. These are called by some Writers, the Intercepted Axes or Intercepted Diameters. V

absis.c: ABSIS, the lame with Apsis ; which see.

absolute.c: ABSOLUTE: This Word (which signifies free from the Power of another) is variously used. Sometimes the Terms of a Proposition are said to be taken Absolutely , that is, without Relation to any thing else. A Prince is said to be Absolute, when he makes his M// his Latv, and will in no respect be restrained or limited by the Laws of his Country. This is otherwise called Arbitrary Power j and arises from ah Imperfection both in the Understanding of the Prince, and in the Spirits of the People. But God Almighty is Absolutefrom the Perfection of his Nature, as containing! in himself all possible Power, and lying under no Limitations nor Restraints from any one. Absolute is sometimes taken also in Opposition to Terms or Conditions; thus God doth not forgive Men their Sins Absolutely, but on Condition «f their Repentance and Amendment; and a Priest cannot absolve Men from the Guilt of their Sins Absolutely, but only deClaratively and ministerially, on the Condition of the Person’s Penitence and Resolutions for Amendment. So (in Law) an Absolute Estate is one free from all manner of Conditions.

absolutenumber.c: ABSOLUTE Number,in an Equation in Algebra, is that which Viet a calls th cHomogcneum Compara - tionis, and which always possesseth one entire part 6r side of the Equation, and is always a known Quantity ; and the Rectangle or Solid, under the unknown Roots, in Quadra ticks and Cubicks. Thus in this Equation aa 11 6 a -=36. The Absolute Number is 36,which is equal to the Product Of the two Roots or Values of a, multiplied one into another.

absoluteequation.c: ABSOLUTE Equation , in Astronomy, is the Aggregate or Sum of the Eccentrick and Optick Equations. See Equation.

absorbents.c: ABSORBENTS, are Medicines that temper and qualific the Acid Juices in the Body, by imbibing or drinking them up. Thus Alkali's are said by some to Absorb Acids.

abstension.c: ABSTENSION, in Law, is a with-holding an Heir from taking possession of his Land.

abstergentorabstersivemedicines.c: ABSTERGENT or Abstersive Medicines, are such as are used to clear the Skin or Superficial Parts of the Body from any Filth, Or. obstructing its Pores.

abstersion.c: ABSTERSION, is the Effect produced by Abstersive Medicines, or in general, any cleansing or wiping away.

abstraction.c: ABSTRACTION, is a Power peculiar to the Mind of Man in contradistinction to the Souls of Beasts, and plainly distinguishing Him from them; whereby he can make his Ideas, arising from particular Things, become general Representatives of all of the same kind. Thus, if my Eye represents to me Whiteness in a Wall, I can Abstractedly consider that Quality of Whiteness, and find it attributable to many other things besides; as to Snow, to Milk, or the like; and this Quality, whatever it be, thus considered apart from the Concrete, or the Subject in which it inheres, is laid to be taken in the Absiratt.

abstract.c: ABSTRACT, is frequently used also for a small Draught or Epitome of any greater Work.

abstractnumbers.c: ABSTRACT Numbers , are those which are considered as Pure Numbers, without being applied to any Subject; and so Abstralled Mathematics, is used in opposition to Mixt Mathematickp ; the former signifying pure Geometry or Algebra ; and the latter Opticks, Dialing, Navigation, Lse. where Physical Considerations are connected with the Mathematical.

abundantnumbers.c: ABUNDANT Numbers, are those whose parts added together make more than the whole Num. her which they are Parts of; as v. g, Twelve, whose Parts being 1, z, z, 4, and 6. these all added together make Sixteen: Thus also the Parts of 20 make zz, G 1 c.

abus.c: ABUS. See Apsis. AB\ SS, is any vast deep place which either hath no Bottom, or else hath none discernible ; or at least is supposed to have none. The Learned Dr. Woodward in his Natural History of the Earth, p. 117. tells us, That there is a mighty Collection of Waters inclosed in the Bowels of the Earth, constituting an huge Orb in the Interiour or Central Parts of it; and over the Surface of this Water he supposes the Terrestrial Strata to be expanded 7 This is what Moses calls the Great Deep, and what many Authors call the Abyss. And that there is such a vast Collection of Waters lodged in the Bowels of the Earth is confirmed by abundance of Observations. The Water of this vast Abyss the Pr. asserts, doth communicate with that of the Ocean by means of certain Holes, Hiatus's or Chasms, palling betwixt it and the Bottom of the Ocean: And this and the Abyss he supposes to have one common Centre, around which the Water of both of them is placed; but so, that the ordinary Surface of the Abyss is not level with that of the Ocean, nor at so great a distance from the Centre as that is, it being for the most part restrained and depressed by the Strata ot Earth lying upon it ; but where-ever those Strata's are broken, or so lax and parole that Water can pervade them, then the Water of the Abyss doth ascend, fills up all the Clefts or Fissures whereinto it can get admittance or entrance , and saturates all the Interstices and Pores of the Earth, Stone, or other Matter, all around the Globe, quite up to the Level of the Ocean.

academy.c: ACADEMY, is a kind of higher School or University, where young Men are instructed in the Liberal Arts and Sciences. ’Twas so called at first from Academia , the Name of a Place near Athens, and built, say some, by Cadmus the Phœnician ; others, by one Academus , whence ic had its Name: ’Twas planted with Trees; and here Plato taught his Disciples Philosophy, who from hence are called Academic fs. Cicero also called one of his Country Seats by this Name, where he had fine Groves, and pleasant Walks for the Entertainment of his Philosophical Friends ; and here he wrote his Books, De Nat. Deorum, and De Amicitia, and his Offices, which therefore he called his Academical Treatises.

academicks.c:
ACADEMICKS; so the Followers of Plato were anciently called, because they studied in the Academia. Afterward ic became the Name of a Sect of Sceptical Philosophers , who maintained, That all things were uncertain, and that Reason and Truth were changeable, so that Men ought to doubt of every thing, and believe nothing. A.CANTABOLUS, the same with Vo[fclla (excepting that the Volsclla is crooked) a Surgeon’s Instrument

A C C A C C Instrument to take out any thing that shall happen to stick in the Oesophagus or Gullet; ’tis something like a pair of Plyers; and may be reckoned as a kind.of Forceps,

acantha.c: ACANTHA, is with some Anatomists, the most backward Protuberance of the Vertebres of the Back, and is otherwise called, Spin a Dors.

acatalectickverse.c: ACATALECTICK Verse, is one exactly perfect, where not so much as one Syllable is either redundant or deficient.

accedasadcuriam.c: ACCEDAS ad Curiam ; a Writ made out of the Chancery and Returnable in the King’s Bench or Common Pleas, and directed to the Sheriff, requiring him to go to the Court of some Lord, or Franchise, (where a Plaint is sued for taking of Cattle as a Distress, or any false Judgment supposed to be made in any Suit in such a Court* which is not a Court of Record) and there make a Record of the said Suit in presence of the Suitors of the laid Court, and also oi four other Knights of the same County; and to cer tile it into the King’s Court, at the Day limited in the W rir.

accedasadvicecomitcm.c: ACCEDAS ad Vice Comitcm, is a Writ directed to the Coroner, requiring him to deliver a Writ to the Sheriff, who having a Pone delivered to him, suppresses it.

accelerationoftiredescentofheavyboiies.c:
ACCELERATION of tire Descent of heavy BoJies was first discovered by GaliLcu: : And if due attention be given to our excellent Mr. If, N:w on s Second Law of Motion, Axiom, or Lave of Nature, as it may be called, vi%, That the mutation of Motion is always proportionable to the Force impressed, and always is according th that same Line of Dire rian , the Reason of the Acceptation of the Descent of heavy Bodies will be very clear and intelligible. For, supposing Gravity (whatever it be) to act uniformly on all Bodies at equal distances from the earth's Centre, and that the Time in which any heavy Body falls to the Earth be divided into equal parts infinitely small: Let Gravity enc line the Body towards the Earth’s Centre while it moves in the first infinitely small part of the Time of its Descent: If after this, the Action of Gravity be supposed to cease, the Body would go towards the Earth’s Centre equally, with a Velocity equal to the Force of that first Impression, (by Mr. Newton's first Axiom.J But now since the Action of Gravity still continues; in the second Moment of Time the Body will receive a new Impulse downward, and then its Velocity will be double of what it was in the first Moment : In the third Moment or Particle of Time it will be Triple; in the fourth Quadruple, and so on continually. Wherefore since theie Particles, of time are up posed infinitely small, and all equal to one another, the Impetus acquired by the Falling Body will be every where as the Times from the beginning of the Descent. And unce the Quantity of Matter in the Body given, continues the same, the Velocity will be as sise Time in which it is acquired (as you will find proved in the Laws of Motion.) And after the lame manner may it be proved, •Ihat the Motion of Ascending Projectives shall be equably retarded ; for since the Force of Gravity acts continually and equally against the Motion first begun, it must diminith or abate the Motion, according to the Time of the Ascent, till at last it wholly cease. accentingrammar.c: ACCENT in Grammar, is a Mark placed over a Syllable to shew ‘tis th be pronounced with a stronger or weaker Voice. The Greeks who wei e the greatest observers of Accents, distinguish them into the Acme one marked thus, ('), the Grave one thus ( ), and the Circumflex thus, ("). But of late one llennin a Dutci -man hath written a Book, to prove, the Accents were not Ancient among the Greeks, and that that Language ought not to be pronounced according to them : He pretends no Accents are to be found in any MbS. above 800 Years old, and takes them to be an Invention of the Arabs about the time of Mahomet’s Death. He says, the MafJ'oretes of Tiberias brought them into. the Bible about the Sixth Century, and that they were perfected by flabby Judah Pen David Chiug, born in pe^, about the Eleventh Century.

accents.c: ACCENTS, in Grammar, shew how to judge of the Measure of Time, in which each Letter, Syllabic, Word, or Expression is pronounced ; the Elevations and Depressions of the Voice, the Silence or Repose of the Voice at the end of Words or Sentences, £?c. These Accents may be very numerous: There are in the Hebrew Grammars more than Thirty of them; and Servius Honor at us reckons Eight in the Latin. The Acute Accent shews when the Voice is to be raised, and is expressed thus ( The Grave Accent shows when the Voice is to be depressed, and is figured thus ('). The Circumflex Accent is compos’d of both the Acute and the Grave, and is expressed thus, ('). The Long Accent , scows that the Voice is to stop upon the Vowel that has that mark, and it is expressed thus, (*}. The Short ylccent, scows that the time of Pronunciation ought to be fhprr, and is marked thus, ("*)._ . ^ Hyphen is an Accent in Grammar, that implies two words are to be joyned, as male-sanus. Diastole, is an Accent in Grammar, Whichihows, that those Words or Sentences to which it is adjoined arc to be separated, its mark is ( ,). accident.c: ACCIDENT: This word is used by Logicians in three Senses. I. In opposition to the Essence of any 1 king, whatever doth not essentially belong to it may (tho* a Substance it self) yet be an Accident or Adjunct to that Thing, or belong to it only accidentally, as the Clothes a Man bath on; the Money in his Purse, &c. These indeed are more properly called Adjuncts ; and by the Schoolmen arc distinguished by the Name of Verbal Accidents. L. In Contradistinction to the Essential Properties of any Subject, many Qualities are called Accidents ; because they are there not Essentially But Accidentally, This in the Schools is called Accidens Predicabilis, and implies a Common Quality, which may or may not be in any Subject, a s any particular Colour, &c. 3. In opposition to Substance, a Thing is called an Accident when it is its Essence or Nature to Inhere or subsist in some Substance, and cannot be alone and thus it is with all Qualities whatsoever. This is called Accidens Predicament ale, and the nine last Predicaments are in this sense Accidents. In reference to its Cause also, or at least as to Knowledge of it, a Thing is frequently sti sod an Accident by which we mean an Effect either casually produced, or which to us appears tp have been so.

accretion.c: ACCRETION; nearly of the same Sense with Augmentation, and is properly an Addition of Matter to any Body externally: This is usually laid ot the encrease of Bodies without Life, and is sometimes called Apposition or su,xta Position. But some will have the encrease <?f Living Bodies to be by Intrcjumption and Assimilation of the Alimentary or nourilliing Particles, Dr. Havers in his Oftcologia gives this Acctount of Accretion , That the Nutritious Particles being separated by the Glandu.es placed, every where on the sides of the Arteries, are carried into those small Nervous Pipes, or Interstices of the Fibres, where the Spirits move, so that they fall in the way of the Spirits Motion: These Spirits he supposes to have a twofold Motion; one direct, the other Potatory or turning round their Axes. While an Animal is capable of Accretion, and the Particles of which the solid Parts consist are not entirely united at their Extremities, but are capable of receding one from another, both endways and literally ; the Spirits act upon the Nutritious Particles (which arc of a Viscous Nature) by their Rotatory Motion, by which they carry them to the sides of the Fibres and Bony Strings, driving some against the sides of their Parts, and forcing them out laterally : Others' they drive into the Interstices between the Extremities, thereby lengthening every Series of them ; where they are placed and fixed, and thus the Parts of an Animal Body increase both in Thickness and Longitude. But after the Particles are united at their Extremities, and no longer capable. of making Room to lodge the Nutritious Parts out of the way of the Spirits direct Motion ; then the Spirits come to act upon the Nutritious Matter by that motion, and to drive ic so through the Nervous Channels, that it has not the liberty of stopping and adhereings and so the Accretion of the Animal ceases. ,

achor.c: ACHOR, is a sort of a crusted Scab which makes an Itching and Stink on the Surface of the Head, and is occasioned by a Serous, Salt and Sharp Matter: The difference betwixt an Acker and Favus consists in this, that in Achors the Holes or Cavities are small, and sometimes not visible j but in a Favus they are more large and conspicuous.

achlys.c: ACHLYS, according to some, is a kind of Darkness in the Eyes, accounted one of the Species of Amblyepia , or Dimness of Sight.

acids.c: ACIDS, whole Particles are supposed to be longifh, flexible, penetrating, and attenuating; and which have their Points sharp and piercing. And these are either Natural Acids ; which have a Proper Acidity of their own without the help of Art, as Juice of Limons, (3 c. or el fe Artificial Acids ; which are made by Fire in Chymical Operations. So that Acid Spirits or Stygian Liquors, as the Chymists call them, from their Powers to destroy or dissolve Bodies, seem to be nothing but an Acid Salt dissolved and put into a violent Motion' by the Fire these are called Acid MetiJlruums. You may easily know whether any Liquor contain in it an Acid Salt or not; by dropping some of it on a little Syrup of Violets spread on White Paper; or into a Solution of Blue-bottle Flowers, (3c. for then the Blue will be immediately turned into a Red or reddish Purple Colour ; whereas if it turn Green, ‘tis a sign the Liquor abounds with Salts of an Urinous or Lixiviate Nature; which how to distinguish,/re these Words. adducentmuscles.c: ADDUCENT MUSCLES, are those that bring forward, close, or draw together the Parts of the Body whereto they are annexed.

adductoroculi.c: ADDUCTOR OCULI, is a Muscle of the Eye ; so called because it inclines its Pupil towards the Nose; and also Bibitorius, it directing the Eye towards the Cup.

adductorpollicis.c: ADDUCTOR POLLICIS, is a Muscle of the Thumb, which arises Tendinous in common with the Abductor Indicts, becoming fleshy, ascends obliquely to its broad Termination at the superior part of the first Bone of the Thumb. This brings the Thumb nearer the Fore-finger.

adductorpollicispedis.c: ADDUCTOR POLLICIS PED1S, is a Muscle of the Great-Toe, which ariseth partly Tendinous and partly Fleshy from the Inferior Parts of the Os Cuneiforme Tertium, and dilating its self to a fleshy Belly, marcheth obliquely in the bottom of the Foot, and becomes less and tendinous at its Insertion to the Internal part of the Ossa Sessamoidea of the Great-Toe laterally opposite to the Termination of the Abductor Pollicis Pedis. This brings the Great-Toe nearer the rest.

aden.c: ADEN, is the Term for a Glandule in an Animal Body, which is either Conglobated , as the Glands of the Mesentery , &c. or else Conglomerated as the Salivas Glands, (sic. With some also ’tis used for a Tumour in the Groin, the same with Bubo.

adepsorpinguedo.c: ADEPS or Pinguedo, Fat, is a similar part of the Body : But Adept and Pinguedo differ in this, that Adeps is a ihicker, harder, and more Earthly Substance than Pinguedo ; the Fat which is particularly meant by Adeps , flows from the Blood through peculiar Vessels into Bags or Bladders appropriate thereunto, as is plain from the Observation of Malpighius. adequate.c: ADEQUATE ; a thing is said to be adequate to, or adequately to agree with another, when *tis every way equal to it in Extent, Capacity, Power, G?e. and all other Properties; and neither exceeds it nor falls short of it in any respect. And thus when the Notions or Ideas that we have of any thing take in all the Properties of that thing, and that we omit conceiving nothing which bclorigs to it, we then say that we have Adequate Ideas of such things.

adequateideas.c: ADEQUATE IDEAS, are those Ideas which perfectly represent the Arch hypes or Images, which the Mind supposes them to be taken from ; which it intends them co stand for, and to which it refers them.

AD Sal’HOROUS, or Neutral, i.e. indifferent: So Mr. Boyle calls a kind of Spirit which he distilled from Tartar and some other Vegetable Bodies j which was neither Acid , Vinous, nor ZJrinous. ’Tis made thus; First, Shavings of Box, Guajacum, or any such ponderous AVood are distilled per fe in a Retort; and then the sowrisli Liquor is rectified to free it from the Phlegm : After this a Quantity of Powder of Coral, &c. was thrown into the sowre Spirit, which, it readily dissolved ; and the Acid Parts of the Menstruum did so associate themselves with the Coral as th leave a part of, the Liquor, that was by no means of an Acid Nature, but which when gently drawn off the Coral, was of a strong Smell, I’et without any Acidity, and in many respects us a different Nature from almost any other common Spirit.

adinquirendum.c: AD INQUIRENDUM, a Writ in Law com- ] banding an Enquiry to be made (for the better Execution of Justice) about the Merits of a Cause upending in the King’s Court.

adjoininganglesingeometry.c: ADJOINING ANGLES in GeometrySec Angles or Contiguous.

adiournment.c: ADJOURNMENT, is the putting off of any Court or meeting, and appointing it to be kept at another Place or Time.

adiposavena.c: ADIPOSA VENA, or Kcnalis, a Vein arising rom the descending Trunk of the Cavd ; which P rc ^ S - self on the Coat, and Fat, that covers the Kidneys.

adiposiductus.c: AD1POSI DUCTUS, called zfoSacculi, Vestcule Adipose or Lobuli, are Vessels which convey the Adcps or Eat into the Interstices of the Muscles, or to the Parts between the Elelh and the Skin.

adit.c: ADIT, is the Shaft, or Entrance into any Mine.

adiudge.c: ADJUDGE, when a determinate Sentence is 'alt in the behalf of another, the Cafe is said ro e Adjudged for him.

adiunct.c: ADJUNCT: Whatever comes to any Being from without is called an Adj mil to that Being ; as being not naturally and essentially belonging to it, but adjoined sr superadded to it. AD JURA REGIS, is a Writ that lies for the Kings Clerk against him that fought to eject him, to the Prejudice of the Kings Title in Right of his Crown.

adiutant.c: ADJUTANT, an Officer in the Army, the same with an Aidc-Major : which see.

admeasurementofdover.c: ADMEASUREMENT of Dover, IS a Writ that lies where a Woman is endowed by an Infant, or by a Guardian of more than she ought to have. Admeasurement of Pasture , is a Writ that lies against such, as having Common of Pasture appendant to their Frcc-holds, do surcharge it with more Cattle than they ought to do.

administration.c: ADMINISTRATION (in Law) is the disposing of a Man’s Goods or Estate that died intestate, or without any Witt, with an intent to give an Account thereof.

administrator.c: ADMINISTRATOR, he that has the Goods of a Man dying intestate, committed to his Charge by the Ordinary, and is accountable for the same. If the Person be a Woman, she is called an Admiuiftratrix.

admittendoclerico.c: ADMITTENDO CLERICO, is a Writ granted to him that hath recovered his right of Presentation against the Bishop, in the Common Bench.

admittendoinsocium.c: ADMITTENDO in Socium , is a Writ for the Association of certain Persons to Justices of Assize before appointed.

adnatatunica.c: ADNATA TUNICA, is the common Membrane of the Eye, called Conjunillvc, it springs from the Skull, grows to the Exterior part ot the Tunica Cornea ; and that the visible Species may pass there, leaves a round Cavity forward, to which is annexed another Tunic, without any particular Name,made up ox the Tendons of those Muscles which move the Eye; by reason of its Whiteness, ’tis called Albuginea. AD OCTO ; among some of the Ancient Philosophers, is a Term signifying the Highest or Superlative Degree ; because they reckoned no Degree above the Eighth, in their way of distinguishing of Qualities.

adonick.c:
ADON1CK, a sort of a short Verse, consisting of a Dailyle and a Spondee ; as, Kara juven - tus ; ’ris usually placed at the end of each Stanza of Saphick Verses. So called from Adonis , in whose praise they were first made. AD QUOD DAMNUM, is a Writ which ought to be sued before the King grant certain Liberties, as a Fair, Market, &c. to the Prejudice of others. There is also another Writ of Ad quod Dam-' num, if any one will turn a Common High-way, and lay out another as beneficial, ADRAMlRE: see Arraign. AD TERMlNtJM qui pmeriitj is a Writ of C x Entry,

ADV ÆRA Entry chat lies where a Man having leafed Lands j great Benefactors to it these were sometimes cal- ‘ Tenements for Life or Years, and after the led Patroni, and sometimes Advocatt. .Now in the . ' ' - rT ’- 'General, an Advowson is where a Bishop, Dean Term expired, is held from them by the Tenant, or other Stranger that occupieth the same, and dcforceth the Lessor in such cafe this Writ lieth for the Lessor and his Heirs.

advanceditch.c: ADVANCE DITCH, in Fortification, isa Ditch dug all along the Glacis beyond the Counterscarps and usually filled with Water.

advanceguard.c: ADVANCE GUARD, is the first Line or Division of an Army ranged or marching in Battlearay ; or that part which is next to the Enemy, or which marches first towards them. The whole Body of any Army consists of the Advance Guard, the Arriere Guard , and the Main Body. Sometime also a Party of i 5 or xo Horse commanded by a Lieutenant beyond, but within sight of the Main Guard, is called an Advance Guard, and is designed for the greater Security of the Camp.

advent.c: ADVENT, in the Sacred Calender, is the Time from the Sunday that falls either upon St Andrerv’s Day or next to it, till Chrijimafs ; which time was wont anciently to be spent in a j?ious Preparation for the Advent or coming on of the Feast of our Saviour’s Nativity.

adventitiabona.c: ADVENT1TIA BONA, were anciently such as came to a Man unexpectedly ; Windfalls, as we call them now hence she word Adventitious comes to be used by Philosophic^ Writers, and to signifie such Matter as doth not properly belong to any mix’d Body, but comes to it from some other place. Thus his a Question, whether in the Freezing of Water, there do not enter in some Frigorific!^ Particles which are Adventitious to the Water, from the Air, or the Freezing Mixture. AD VENTREM INSPICIENDUM, isa Writ mentioned in the Statute of Essoignes: see Venire Infpiciendo •

adverb.c: ADVERB, in Grammar, is a part of Speech undeclined, and without Conjugation; and is usually joined with a Verb to express the manner of Action. They are distinguished into Adverbs of Time , Place , &c. ‘ ADULTERATION of any Thing, such as Wine, Medicinal Druggs, Chymical Preparations, Gfc. is a mixing some Baler Matter with ir, which hinders it from being truly Good and Genuine in its kind.

advocates.c: ADVOCATES, in the Ecclesiastical Court, were either Advocate of the Causes and Interest of the Church, retained as a Counsellor and Pleader, to maintain the Properties and Rights: Or, Advocate or Patron of the Presentation and Advowson. Both these Offices did formerly belong to the lame Founder of a Church or Covenr, and his Heirs, who were bound to protect and defend the Church, as well as to nominate or present to it. But when the Patrons grew negligent, or were Men of no Interest or Ability in the Courts of Justice, then the Religious began to retain a Law Advocate , to follicite and prosecute their Controversial Causes. See Spelman.

advowson.c: ADVOWSON, in our Common Law signifies a right to present to a Benefice, and is as much as Jus Patronattts in the Canon Law ; the Realism why *tis termed Advowson ( Advocatio ) is. because anciently those who had a right to present to a Church, were Maintainers of it, or or Chapter, and their Successors, or any Lay Patron, have a Right to present, whom they please, to any Spiritual Benefice, when it becomes void. Advowjon is of two sons; First, Advowson in Gross, that is, sole or principal, nor belonging to any Marmot, as a Parcel of its right: Secondly, Advowson Appendant, which depends upon a Mannor, as appurtenant to it; and this may be sold by it self, and then it is in Gross And while it is dependant to the Marmot, ’tis by Kftchin called an Incident.

adust.c: ADUST, burnt or parched; the Blood is said to be Adust, when by reason of extraordinary Heat, the thinner parts are steem’d forth, and the thicker remain dreggy and black, as if they were burnt.

gylops.c: ÆGYLOPS, Angilops and Anchylops, is a Tumour or Swelling in the great corner of the Eye by the Root of the Nole, either with or without an Inflammation.

gytiacum.c: ÆGYTIACUM, fc. Unguentum, in Pharmacy, is a kind of Detersive Ointment described by Iviesuc ; and is so called from its black Colour, like the Hue of an Egyptian.

olipile.c: ÆOLIPILE, is a round hollow empty Ball made of Iron, Brass, Copper, Gc. and furnished with a Neck in which there is a very slender Pipe opening into the Ball. Sometimes the Neck is made to screw into the Ball; which is the best way, because then the Cavity may the more readily be filled with Water. But if there be no Screw, you must fill it with Water, thus; Heat the Ball red hot, and then throw it into a Vessel of Water; the Water will run in at the small Hole and fill about | of the Cavity. And if after this the Æolipile be laid on or before the Fire, so that the Water and Vessel become very much heated, the Vaporous Air will be forced out with very great Noise and Violence ; but it will be by fits, and not with a constant and uniform Blast. Perhaps they may be sometimes of use to blow the Fire, where a very quick and strong Blast is required. And they may serve to scent or perfume a Room by filling them with Perfumed, instead of common Water.

quilibrium.c: ÆQULIBR1UM, is when either equal Weights at equal Distances, or unequal ones at reciprocally proportionable Distances from the Centre, make the Arms of any Libra or Balance to hang even ; so that they do Equiponderate and not out-weigh one another: In such a Cafe we say the Balance is in Æquilibrio, ÆQUIVOCAL: See Equivocal.

ra.c:
ÆRA: Lucilius and some others say, that Æra did originally signify a Number stamp’d on Money to determine its current Value ; and in this Sense it comes from Æs Brass, from the Plural of which Æra, came this feminine singular Æra: and that either because they put the word Æra to each particular of an Account as we now do Item : Or else because the Number of Years was anciently among the Ramans mark’d down in Tables with little Brass Nails. In reference to which latter Custom the word Æra came to . . signisi*

Æ T A A b F signifie the same with Epocha, vi\. a certain Time or Date from whence to begin the New Year ; or some particular way of reckoning Time and Years. And in this Signification the word is j thought to arise from these Initial Letters, A. E. H. A. which among the Spaniards , who began ‘ their Æra from the Reign of Augufius , stood for , Annus er at stegni Augusti. The most eminent j Æra’s among Chronoiogers, are the Æra of the World’s Creation, which according to the Julian Account of Time began in the Month ot Otlober, and on the 24th Day. Some place this 3950 Years before Christ's Birth, whom Gajsendus faith, come nearest to truth, and that this Æra is confirmed by the French Astronomers ; others account 3983 Years before the Birth of our Saviour, and with these Petavius joins. Kepler makes them 3993 ; and there are some who will have it, that the true Number is 5199. The Jewish Æra or Period, invented by Hi de I about the Year of Christ 344. This is by no means Historical , but Artificial and Astronomical* and is suited to the Jews false Account of the New Moons, Feasts, Holidays, and is of far later standing than the beginning of the World, tho’ they use it as the Date of the Creation j it begins in Autumn. The Æra from the Dettrtiction of Troy, begins June 16. as Scaliger proves out of Ephortts : cis very common in Profane Authors, The Æra of Nabonaffar begins the 26th of February (747 Years before Christ) but it varieth in 1461 Years thro* the whole 365 Days; for so many he accounts, neglecting the odd Hours, which makes a great Intercalation . The Æra of the Olympiads begins from the New Moon in the Summer Solstice 777 Years before Christ, and theÆnt of Iphitus is only a Collection of the Olympick Years : These two are the Æra’s chiefly used by Greek Historians. The Epman Æra, from the building of the City, begins April 21. and is 752 Years before Christ. The Christian Æra from the Birth of Christ begins December 25. The Turkish Æra or the Hegira, begins the 16th Day of July ; they account it from Mahomet's Slight, A. D. 622. The Æra of the Death of Alexander the Great is the 1 ach of November, 324 Years before Christ. See Epocha. ÆS USTUM, or calcin’d Copper is made by Stratifying Plates of Copper with Powder of Sulphur in ,a Crucible, whole Cover or Lid hath a Hole in it, to give the Vapours Vent, while the Matter is Calcining in a strong Fire, till no more Fumes will arise ; the Plates must lie separated while hot. In this Stratification the first and last Beds or Layers must be of Sulphur.

schynomenousplants.c: ÆSCHYNOMENOUS PLANTS, the same as Sensitive ; which see.

stivalsolstice.c: ÆSTIVAL SOLSTICE, or Summer Solstice: See Solstice.

tateprobanda.c: ÆTATE PROBANDA, is a Writ of Office, and st lses for the Heir of the Tenant that held of the King in chief, to prove that he is of full directed to the Sheriff to enquire of his "g e » and then he shall become Tenant to the f^ ln 8 by the same Services that his Ancestors made to the King.

ther.c: ÆTHER : Dr. Hoot^ Microgr. p. 13. calls the Æther that Medium or Fluid Body in which all other Bodies do as it were swim and move. But this seems to me co favour the Cartesian Dothine of an Absolute Plenum, which by many Infallible Reasons and Experiments is proved to be impossible. As therefore we call the Medium in which we breath and live, the Air, by which we understand an Elasticai Fluid Body, either having its very large Interstices devoid of all Matter, or else filled in part with a Fluid which is very easily moved out of them by Compression, and which readily returns into them again when that Compression is taken off: So we agree to call that finer Fluid Body, if it be a Body, which is extended round our Air and Atmosphere, above it anti beyond it, up to the Planets, or to an Indefinite Distance; this, I say, we call the Æther , tho* what we mean by that word, we scarce well understand. For that there can be no Fluid whose parts do resist the Motions of Bodies thro’ them (as our Air doth) in the Planetary Regions, we are certain almost to a Demonstration ; because the Motion of the Heavenly Bodies is by no means impeded or altered by any such Residence, but they move as freely as if they were in an absolute Void. But that which is often meant by the word Æther or Æthereal Matter, is a very fine thin Diaphanous Fluid, which some will have to surround the Earth up to as far as the Interstcllary World, and which easily penetrates and runs thro’ all things, and lets all things run as easily thro’ it.

thiopsmineral.c: ÆTHIOPS MINERAL, is a Medicine usually made by Incorporating well together equal parts of Running Mercury and Fiower of Sulphur, and then deflagrating the Mixture. But 'cis much the best way only to mix them well together in a Glass Mortar, and never to enkindle the Matter at all; the Mercury will perfectly disappear, and the Powder in a little rime will turn black.

tiology.c: ÆTIOLOGY, signifies an Account of the Causes and Reasons of Diseases, and of their various Symptoms, in order to their Cure: Wherefore it is by some called Pathology.

affeerors.c: AFFEERORS, a Term in Law, signifies such as are appointed in Court-leets, &c. upon Oath to mulct those who have committed any Fault which is arbitrably punishable, and for which no express Penalty is prescribed by Statute. To AJfere an Amercements is properly to lessen and mitigate the Rigour of it.

affiance.c: AFFIANCE (in Law) is the plighting of Troth between a Man and awe man upon an Agreement of Marriage to be had between them.

affidavit.c: AFFIDAVIT, in Law, signifies an Oath, as to make Affidavit , is to test isle a thing upon Oath.

afforciament.c: AFFORCIAMENT, a Fortress or Strong Hold, or other Fortification.

afforest.c: AFFOREST, (a term in the Forest Law) signifies to lay waste a piece of Ground, and turn it into Forest.

affrayoraflraiment.c:
AFFRAY or Aflraiment, in the Common-Law,' is an Affrightmenr put upon one or more Persons ; and this may be wrought, they say, without a Word spoken, or Blow given: As if a Man should shew himself in Armour, or furnished with Weapons not usually worn, it may strike a Fear int®

A I D A 1 R into others that are unarmed ; which therefore is a Common Wrong, and is inquirable in a Courtleet, wheicin it differs from an Assault , which is always a Particular Injury,

affretamentum.c: AFFRETAMENTUM, the Freight of a Ship from the French Fret , which signifies the Tuns.

ageprieratermincommonlaw.h: AGE PRIER a Term in Common Law
ageprieratermincommonlaw.c: AGE FRIER {a Term in Common Law J is when an Action is brought in against an Infant for Land which he hath by descent, for then he is to stew the matter to the Court, and stall pray that me Action may be stay’d till his full age of 21 Years, and so by Award of the Court the Suit stall surcease.

agentandpatient.c: AGENT and PATIENT (in Common-LawJ is, when a Man is the Doer of a thing, and the Party to whom it is done; as where a Woman endows her self of the fairest Possession of her Husband.

aggregate.c: AGGREGATE, is much the same as the Summ, arising from the Addition, Connexion or Collection of several things together.

aggressesorogreiies.c: AGGRESSES or OgreJJes, the same with Pellets. A Term in Heraldry : See Balls.

aggressor.c: AGGRESSOR, is he that makes the first assault, attack, or that first begins any Quarrel, Encounter, or Difference.

agild.c: AGILD, in Law, signifies free from Penalty, not subject to the customary Fine or Imposition.

agistaterminlaw.c: AGIST sa Term in Law) signifies, to take in, and feed the Cattle of Strangers in the King’s Forest, and to gather Money due for the same to the King’s use. The Officers doing it arc called,

agisters.c: AGISTERS ; and their Office is called, AGISTMENT.

agitation.c: AGITATION, in general, signifies Motion or Action ; but ’tis mostly used in a Philosophical Sense for the brisk Intestine Motion of the small I Corpuscles of any Natural Body. Thus Fire or Heat agitates the small Particles of all Bodies, and puts them into a Rapid Motion.

agnation.c: AGNATION, in the Civil Law, is the Term for that Line of Consanguinity which is between Males descended from the same Father; as Cognation is the Line of Parentage between Males and Females, both descended from the same Father. The Use of both these Words is derived from the old Ityman Law.

agriculture.c: AGRICULTURE, is the Art of Tilling, Manuring, and Cultivating the Earth, in order to render it fertile, and to make it bear Plants, Trees and Fruits.

agrypnia.c: AGRYPNIA , is a kind of Coma Vigil , a Watching or Dreaming Slumber, proceeding from some Disorder in the Brain.

agrypnocoma.c: AGRYP.NOCOMA , the same with Coma Vigil. AIDE DE CAMP, in an Army is an Officer always following one of the Generals; i. e. the General, Lieutenant General, or Major General, to receive and carry their Orders as Occasion requires. When the King is in the Field, he usu-i ally appoints young Gentlemen of Note to carry his Orders, and they are called, th e King's Aides dc Camp.

aidemaiororadjutant.c: AIDE MAJOR or Adjutant , is an Officer whose Business it is to cafe the Major of part of his Duty, and to perform it all in his Absence, Some Majors have several Aides Majors, each Troop of Guards hath but one Major, who hath two Aides Majors under him, according to the greatness of the Business every Regiment of Foot hath as many Aides A Fa j or s as it contains Batallions. When the Batallion is drawn up the Aide Majors Post is on the Left beyond all the Captains, and behind the Lieutenant Colonel.

aile.c: AILE, is a Writ which Les where Land descends from the Grandfather to the Son or Daughter of his Son, these that being dead before the entry by him, and one abates, the Heir stall have this Writ against the Aba tor.

For 284 is equal to the J Summ of all the Aliquot Parrs of the second Number 220, which are 1, 2, 4, 5 10, 11, ao, 22, 44, 55, no. and the latter Number 220 is equal to all the Aliquot Parts of 284, wsif. 1, 2, 4 > 7 i, 142AIR. The Atmospherical Air in which we i bi ‘ath is a Diaphanous, Compressible and Dilatable Fluid Body, covering the Earth and Sea to a great height above the highest Mountains; and differs from the Æther (among other things) in this, that it Refracts the Rays of the Moon and other Remoter Luminaries. This Air seems to consist of 3 differing Kinds of Corpuscles, or small Bodies, 1. Such as are carried up into it in the Form of Exhalations or Vapours from the Earth, Sea, and all Animal, Vegetable and Mineral Bodies, by means of the Sun’s, or the Subtcrrancal Heat. 1. There are yet a more subtle sort of Particles in the Air, which we may reckon emitted into it from the Heavenly Bodies; and also the Magnetick Steams of this Globe of Earth and Water. But 3, There is also a Third kind of Particles, which perhaps do most properly merit the Name of Aereal, as being the proper and distinguishing Parts of Air taken in the strictest sense; and these are Corpulcies which arc constantly FJastical or Springy • For Elasticity is an Essential Property of Air, and I believe no other Fluid hath any thing of it but only so far as it participates of Air, or hath Air contained in its Pores. So that our Air certainly doth either consist of, or abound with Parts of such a Nature, that in case they be bent or compressed by the Weight of the incumbent part of the Atmosphere, or of any other Body, they do endeavour to free themselves from that pressure, by bearing against the Bodies that keep them bent; and as loon as these Bodies are removed to give them way, they use end themselves, either quite, or so far forth as the Bodies that resist them will permit, and thereby expand the whole parcel of Air, these Elastical Bodies compose. Dr. Hoof in his Micrograph, p. 13. seems to think the Air to be nothing else but a kind of Tincture or Solution of Terrestrial and Aqueous Particles dissolved in, and agitated by the Æther; and these Particles he supposes to be of a Saline nature, Mr. Boyle found, that one and the some portion of Air may take up 5&0000 times the Space it doth

A I R A I R doth at another time. See Trails about the admirable Rarefaction of the Air, And in the laid Discourse he tells us, That he found by undoubted Experiments, that the same quantity of Air, by only having the Pressure of the Atmoiphcre taken off in the Pneumatick Ingine, and without any Adventitious Heat to enc reate its Spring, would possess above 13000 times its natural Space or Dimensions. Dr. Gregory in his Astron. p. 401. shews, that if Air expand it self according to Mr. Boyl' s observed Law; vis'. That the Spaces into which it may be compressed are always reciprocally proportional to the compressing weight: 1 hen a Globed Air of the Diameter of one Inch, if rarefied so, as (according to that Rule) it must be at the distance of the Earth’s Semi-diameter (from the Earth) will fill all the Planetary Regions as far as, and much beyond, the Sphere of Saturn, And the great Dilatation and Compression of Air may be easily enough conceived .without the Intervention of any subtile matter, if we imagine each proper elastick Particle of Air to be like a little ' Spring of a Watch coiled up round, or wound up like a ' piece of Ribband : for, if you allow further, that these Particles have also a Circular Motion round their own Axes, the Parts of each Roll, Coil, or Lamina will endeavour to recede from the Axis of its Motion, and this more or lels according to the Ve.ocity of their Motion ; by which means they will acquire a Springiness outward like a Watch Spring, and will endeavour to fly or unwind themselves out to their full length, but that they are hindered by other such Parades on every side: And therefore these E lastick Particles in the lower Parts of the Atmo sphere will always be kept bent or wound up, by the weight of the whole of the Air; but if at any time they can get rid of this weight and external pressure, they will readily by their natural Spring evolve themselves and extend their Roll, or circles to vastly larger Dimensions. And this may be the reason of the Tumclcence of a Bladder st ot apparently blown cut, in the exhausted Receiver ; of a full-blown one (if dry) breaking there, and of the breaking of square figured Vials , when stopt well, and the Air throughly drawn off from them. And ’tis equally easie to conceive, that a great Dilatation or Rarefaction of Air may be produced % Heat; for the Rapid Motion of the Calorifick Particles must needs so move the Aercal ones, and by that means may make them more endeavour to recede from the Axis of their Motion, and consequently more unwind or unroll themselves; wherefore they must take up more space, and ttiuft more thrust, by this uncreated Spring, all pther Bodies from them, and separate themselves from one another. Mr. Boyle in his Discourse against Sinus shews, mat the Strengths required to compress Air , are in Reciprocal Proportion (nearly) to the Spaces comprehending the same Portion of Air,

AIRS WEIGHT. The Weight of the Air was r st discovered by the great Galli/eus ; who findmg th a t Water by pumping could be raised no cr than 34 or 35 Beet, cone uded, that the sr |i| n ,°f a n infinite fuga vacui would not do in - IS c ant ^ therefore happily fell on thinking foe Counter-Balance of the Air's Weight, which Torricclllus afterwards pursued and improved, with like Sagacity; inventing, as a farther proof of the Notion of the Gravity of the Air, chat which we call the Torricellian Experiment. Mr. Boyle found a Lamb’s Bladder containing about-) of a Pint, and blown up, and well dried to lose about a Grain and -Jwhen it was prickt, and the Air let out. Also, that a Lamb’s Bladder being counterpoized in a nice pair of Scales in the Receiver, on the Air’s being drawn out, did manifestly preponderate j but when the External Air was let in again, the Scales returned to their former Equilibrium. An Æolipile well heated, and then having its little hole stopt, was cooled and weighed j after which the hole being opened, the Air was heard plainly to rush in with a whistling noise, and then the Æolipile being weigh’d again, it was manifestly heavier than it was before. The Magdcburgicl^Engine being weighed when full of Air, and afterwards being again weighed when ’twas well exhausted, was found to weigh an entire Ounce and t 4 less than it did before. And Mr. Boyle found by accurate Experiments, that a small Receiver weigh’d 35 Grains more when full of Air, than after it was exhausted. He found also that A Glass Bubble as big as an Hen’s Egg, having as much Air as could be driven out by Heat, had then its Stem nimbly sealed up, and then being left leisurely to cool (for there is great danger of their breaking) was put into a nice Balance, and then the Scales were equipoized.- After the sealed end being warily broken off, the Air was heard to rutfi in with a whistling Noise, and then the Scale in which the Buble was did manifestly preponderate by near ^ of a Grain. And after this, filling it with Water, it was found to hold 906 Grains of that Liquor ; so that allowing for of the Cavity of the Bubble’s being filled with Air, which perhaps might weigh about a Grain, the Proportion of Water to Air appears in weight to be about 905 to one, and roundly it may be supposed, as 1000 to one, because'tis not possible but that some Air must remain in the Bubble more than is now accounted for. Mr. Boyle found by repeated Experiments, that the weight of Air to Water is as 1000 to 1. Mr. Halley, in Philof. Trans. N°. 181, says, That the Specifick Gravity of the Air, near the Earth’s Surface to that of Water, ac several trials, was as i to 840, as 1 to 852, and as 1 to 860 ; the Mercury standing at all those times about 29-) ; but because ’twas Summer Weather, and consequently the Air rarefied when all these were try’d, it may without sensible Errour in round Numbers, be said, that the Barometer standing at 30 Inches, and in a mean estate of ! Heat and Cold, the Specifick Gravity of the Air j to fVater,is as 1 to 800.- Wherefore, since Mercu- ! ry to Water is as 13 *. to 1, Mercury will be to Air as 10800 to 1, and a Cylinder of Air of ! 10800 Inches or 900 Feet, is equal to an Inch of ' Mercury; wherefore, if the Air were through- , out of an equal Density, the Height of the Atmosphere would be no more than 5 Miles and one Tenth of a Mile, and in the Ascent of every i 900 Feet from the Earth’s Surface, the Mercury in

A I R A i R in rhe Barometer would fall an Inch. But since the Expansion of Air increases as the weight of the Incumbent Atmosphere decreases, or as the Mercury links in the Barometer ; the upper parts of the Air must be much more rarefied than the lower, and consequently the Height of the Atmosphere much greater than 5 Miles.

AIR PUMP. An Instrument to exhaust the Air out of proper Vessels. Mr. Boyle owns he had the first hint of it from Schottus , who had published to the World , ( but Mr. Boyle had not seen the Book) that one Otto Gerick, (Consul of Magdeburgi.\ had found out a way ot evacuating Giafs Vessels, by lucking out the Air at the Mouth of the Vessel, plunged under Water. But this Engine was defective in two respects: 1. That in order to evacuate the Vessel, there was required the continual labour of two strong Men for two Hours. 2. The Receiver and Engine being all of one piece, there was no way to get things in and out of it, in order to try any Experiments upon them. To remedy which, and to supply thole Imperfections which Mr. Boyle had heard the Otto Gerics Engine laboured under, he directed one Mr. G. and Dr. Hoof to contrive a newer and better Air-Pump ; which Dr. Tioos effected in the following form, which I will describe because it was the first of the kind made here. This Air-Pump consists of two Parts; a Glass vessel; and a Pump to draw the Air out of it. The Glass is express 1 d by the Fig. 1. ^ having a Hole at the Top with a Cover fitted to it, and also a Stop-Cock fastened to the extremity of its Neck below; its Cavity being large enough to contain about 60 Ib. of Water. The Diameter (BC) of the Hole at the Top of the Vessel (A) is about four Inches, the Orifice whereof is encompassed with a Lip of about an Inch in height, whole use is for the Cover to rest on; which Cover is described in the Second Figure, where (D E) denotes a Brazen Ring, which is to cover, and to be closely cemented on the Lip (B C) of the first Figure. To the internal tapering Orifice of this Ring is fitted a Brass Stopple (PG) so exact as to prevent any considerable access of External Air: In the midst of this Cover there is a Hole (HI) of about half an Inch Diameter, encompass’d with a Ring or Socket of Brass, to which is likewise fitted a Stopple ( ^) of the same Metal, so exquisitely adapted to it, that it may be turned round without admitting in the least Air, and yet may be put in or taken out at pleasure: Through the lower end of it, there is a little Hole (8) made for the passage of a String, (8, 9, to) which is likewise to pass through a small brazen Ring (L) fixed to the bottom of the Stopple (FG) ; the use of which String is to move what is contained in the exhausted Vessel, without unstopping it. That the Stop cock (S) fin the first Figure) might be better fastened to the Neck and lower Orifice of the Receiver, and more exactly exclude the Air, a thin Plate of Tin (M, T, V, IF ) was soder’d on to the Shank of the Cock (X), of length enough to cover the Neck of the Receiver, and cemented on with Pitch, Rosin and Wood-ashes well incorporated together and poured hor into the Cavity of the Plate; and to prevent the Cement from running into the Orifice ( Z^) of the Shank ( X ) it was stop’d with a Cork, having a String fixed to it, that it might be drawn out at the upper Orifice of the Receiver, and then the Glass Neck of the Receiver being well warmed, and thrust into the Cement, it filled the Interstices betwixt the Tin Plate and the Receiver, as also between the Internal Superficies of the Receiver and the Shank ot the Cock. The lower part is the Sucking-Pump or Air pump , supported by a Frame of Wood , with three Legs ( 111 ) so contrived, for the freer motion of the Hand, that one side of it may stand perpendicular; across the midst of the Frame is nailed a Board, (222) to which th e Pump is fastned. The Pump is made up of four Parts, vi%. An exact and strong Cylinder of Brass of about 14 Inches in length, with a Cavity of about 3 Inches diameter ; to which is fitted a Sucker made upof two Parts; the one (44) somewhat less in Diameter than the Cavity of the Cylinder; on which a thick piece of tanned Leather is nailed, whereby it closes so exactly to the Cylinder, that the Air cannot insinuate it self between them The other part being a thick and narrow Plate of I. ion (55) is firmly joyned to the middle of the former Part (44); it is somewhat longer than the Cylinder; one Edge of it being smooth, but the other indented (as in the Figure) with a row of Teeth ; to the Interstices of which are fitted the Teeth of a small Iron Nutt (LB) which is fastned by two Staples (22) to the under side of the cross Board (222) on which the Cylinder rests, and is turned to and fro by the M-mubrium or Handle (7). The last part of the Pump is the Valve ( 1 ^ ) being a Hole at the Top of the Cylinder, a little taper towards the Cavity ; to this Hole is fitted a Brass Pegg, to be put in or taken out upon occasion. Having thus described the Engine, it will be requisite for the better exclusion of the outward Air, and the more easie moving of the Sucker, Stop-cock and Key S, as also the Valve, that they should be well oiled with Sallad Oyl; but sometimes Oyl and Water together prove more effectual: Also that the Ingress of the Air betwixt the Brass Cover and the Ring may be likewise prevented, the Edges of both must with the former Cement be carefully plaistered, and spread on with a hot Iron, that it may run the better and sill the little Cavities. Things being thus fitted, and the lower Shank (O) of the Stop-cock being put into the upper Orifice of the Cylinder, then the .Handle being turned till rhe Sucker rises to the top of it, and shutting the Valve with the Plug, and turning the other way, the Sucker is drawn down to the bottom ; by which means the Air is driven out of the Cylinder, and a succession from without being prevented, the Cavity of the Cylinder must be emptied of Air; then if the Turn-cock be turned so as to afford a pa stage betwixt the Receiver and Cylinder, part of the Air contained in the Receiver will descend into the Cylinder, and by turning back the Key, that may be prevented from Hying back into the Receiver, and may also by opening the Valve, and winding up the Sucker be forced into the open Air; and so by reiterated exsuctions of the Air out of the Receiver, and Expulsions of it again our of the Cylinder, it may
