albumoculi.c: ALBUM OCULI, sometimes is taken for the same with Albugo : But by Galen and Hippocrates is used sot that Tunick of the Eye which is usually calld, the Tunica Adnata ; and by some Writers Albuginca Oculi : Which fee under those Words.

alcaicks.c: ALCI IAICKS, are a sort of Verses consisting of two Dattyls and two Trochees, as some will have it ; but Fabricius faith, they consist of 5 Beet, of which the first is a Spondee or Iambics, the second an lamb sick , the thifd a long Syllable, the fourth a Datlyle, the fifth a Datlyle or Ampbimacer j as these of Horace. Vides ut alia st at n'tve candidum Soratte, nec jam Justineant onus.

alchymist.c: ALCHYMIST, is one that studies Alchymy ; that is, that Sublimcr Part of Chymistry which teaches the Transmutation of Metals and the Philosopher’s Stone j according to the Cant of the Adcptipts, who amuse the Ignorant and Unthinking with hard Words and Non-sense : For were it not for the^H/^ Particle Al, which they will needs have to be of wonderful vertue here, the word would signifie no more than Chymistry, AVhole Derivation lee under that Word. This Study of Alchymy hath been rightly defined to be, j Ars fine Artc, cujus principium c/t mentire, medium labor arc, (st fir tis mcndicare That is, an Art without an Art, which begins with Lying, is continued with Toil and Labour, and at last ends iu Beggery. And so poor Penotvs found it, Who after he had spent his whole Life and Fortune in this vain Study, died at last in an Almshouse at Tver don in Switzerland ; and used ,to soy, he would recommend the Study of Alchymy so a mortal Enemy, whom he did not da re openly to attack.

alcohol.c: ALCOHOL, a Term used by the Chymists Joth lor a very fine or impalpable Powder ; and, also for a very pure Spirit well recti sym or dcphlegmated. Thus the highest rectify’d Spirit of Wine is called Alcohol Vint, Hence to Alcoholize any thing, with them signifies to subtilize; as when any thing is beaten to a very sine Powder, (&c.. How to make a tolerable true Alcohol or pure Spirit or Wine, fee in Alcalizate Spirit of Wine.

alcove.c: ALCOVE, in Architecture is a part of a Chamber separated by an Estrade or Partition made by Columns and other corresponding Ornaments, in which is placed a Bed of State j or sometimes Seats to entertain Company.

aldebaran.c: ALDEBARAN, an Arabian Name for a fixt Star of thdirst magnitude, situate in the Head of the Constellation cass od the Bull, and therefore is usually named the Bu s s-Eye. Al.E-TASTER, is an Officer appointed and sworn in every Court-Leet, to look that there be a due size and goodness of Bread, Ale and Beer sold within the jurisdiction of thel.eet.

alembick.c: ALEMBICK, is a Chymical Instrument used in Distilling, it has the Shape of an Helmet, Concave within, and Convex without; and towards the bottom is placed a Beek or Nose about a Foot and an half long, by which the Vapours descend ; sometimes they are made without a Nose, but then they are rather Circulatory Vessels, and the Head is called a Blind Head: They are made usually of Copper tin’d within-side ; and often of Glass.

aleophangin.c: ALEOPHANGINÆ ( Pilluhc) are purging Pills competed of Aloes and several Spices. AI.ERSANS JOUR (a Law-term) signifying, to be finally dismiss’d the Court, because there is no further Day assigned for Appearance.

alexipharmickmedicines.c: ALEXIPHARMICK MEDICINES, are such as are used as Antidotes against Poison, or any Infectious Disease ; or to raise or strengthen the decayed or drooping Spirits in malignant Distempers. AI.EXITERICAL"? the same with AlcxipbarALEX1TERICK SmickALGAROT, In Chymistry, signifies a strong Emetick and Cathartick Powder, the lame as Mercurius Vit.v, being made of Butter of Antimony precipitated into a white Powder, by being washed or diluted in a large Quantity of warm Water.

algebra.c:
ALGEBRA ; the wonders ill Analytics Art, or the Art of Equation. In Arabiclg is called , Al-giabr Wal-mokabala , from the former of which words we call it Algebra j and it may be rer.der’d, either, the Art of Rcslitution and Comparison, or the Art of Resolution and Equation. Lucas de Burgo, the most Ancient European Writer of Algebra we have, defines it Rciiaurationts (st Oppojitionis Regula. The Italians give it the Name of Regula Rei (st Census ; that is, the Rule of the Root and the Square , because they call the Root Res and the Square Census , and from Co fa in the Italian Language for Res or the Root, comes the word Costickst For some Writers call the Powers of Numbers, as the Root, the Square, the Cube, 8cc. C(stick. Numbers, Cardan calls it, and that very justly, Ars magna, The great Art ; following therein Lucas de Burgo, who stiles it in Italian, L'Arte Maggiore, It was certainly of Old in use amongst the Grecians, but purposely concealed as a very great Secret. We have some Examples of it in Euclidt or at least in The on upon Euchde, who tells us, it was first communicated by Plato There are also

A L G A L G so Instances of this Art in Pappus ; and we iindj the Effects of it plainly in Archimedes, Apcllonius ,! and some others, tho’ studiously covered and dilj guiled. The first Book among the Greeks , and I believe the only one that treats professedly of Algebra , is that of Diophantus : Publillied at first in Latin by Xylander, afterwards in Greek, and Latin by Bachet with some things added of his own; and since him by Mr. Fermat with some Additions of his likewise. But it certainly was in use among the Arabs more anciently than among the Greek ?; and they are supposed to have had it from the Persians , and the Persians from the Indians. Thence, that is, from the Arabs, the Moors and Saracens brought it into Spain, from whence it came into England ; and that before we knew any thing of Diophantus. The Use of the Numeral Figures, Mathematick Learning, and all our Astronomy, came to us likewise the lame way from the same Original, and about the same Time. The first European Writer of Algebra (as was hinted above) is Lucas Pacciolus or Lucas de Burgo a Minorite Friar: His Book is in Italian, Printed at Venice, 1494. He makes mention of one Lecnardus Pi/anus, and several others from whom he learnt it, but we have none of their Writings. He says, this Art came originally to us from the Arabs, and makes no mention of Diophantus j who therefore ’tis probable was not yet known here. His Algebra goes no farther than Quadratick Equations. Next came out Stiphelius a good Author, but he also went not beyond Quadraticks. But Scipio Ferreus , Cardan , Tartalea , and some others, proceeded to give a Solution of some Cubick Equations. After this Bombelli went a little farther, and shewed how to resolve a Biquadratick Equation into two Quadratick ones, by the means of a Cubick. Then, in the last Century, appeared Nonnius l^Nunnet' in Spanish) Damns, Schonerus, Saliguacus, Clavius, &c. who wrote on this Subject in various ways, but generally went no further than Quadratick Equations. About this time out came Diophantus, whose Method differs much from that of the Arabs, which others had hitherto all followed. All this while, the known Quantities in any Equation were designed only by the Numeral Letters, and there were no Symbals nor Marks but for those that were unknown or sought. But then ctsmcVieta, A. D. 1 590, and introduced what he called his Specious Arithmetick ; which is a way of giving Marks or Symbols to all the Quantities, both known and unknown; whereby a very short and conspicuous way of Notation was gained, the whole Operation exposed always to the Eye in a short Synopsis, and many Discoveries were made in Algebra, not before taken notice of. Viet a also introduced the Numeral Exegesis of ad sect ed Equations, (hewing how to extract their Boots in Numbers. And in the Denomination of the Powers of Numbers he follows Diophantus, tend not the Arabian Manner used by others. The Incomparable Mr. Oughtred followed, and mightily improved the Specious Algebra of Vieta, in his Clavis Mathematica first Published 1631: j He also affecting Brevity, (which indeed he was ! a perfect Master of, being short but not obscure ) ! invented many Compendious Characters ot Ligatures, to note theS«t»mr, Differences, l{ct angles, Squares, Cubes, and their Sum/n, Difference, Sx. by which means his little Book contains more excellent a nd useful Geometry than many other large Volumes. Oughtred in his Clavis usually contents himself with the Solution of Quadraticks, rarciy proceeding to those of higher Powers, because he design’d ic as an Introduction to Algebra only. The famous Mr. Harriott was Contemporary with Oughtred, but died before him; he lest many good things behind him, of which nothing is yet published, but his Analytice or Algebra , which Mr. Warner printed A. D. 1631. From this great Man did Des Cartes borrow, not to lay steal, all the famous things in his Geometry, which are purely Algebraical, as any one may lee that will compare their Methods together: For ’cis impossible but one must be copied after the other: But the Geometry ot Des-Cartes was not publilh'd in French till the Year 1637 ; and not in Latin till the Year 1649 : Therefore he must have seen and copied Harriott’s Book. Mr. Harriott did wonderfully improve (in this Treatise) that which is purely Algebra, in the following Respects, and many others which I might mention. 1. He brought in small Letters instead of the Capitals used by Vieta and Oughtred, 1. He waved the Uncouth Terms of Quadrato-Cubc , Sursolid, &c. explaining the Power plainly to the Eye, by only repeating the Root as often as the Index of the Power. 3. He (hewed the true Original and Constitution of all Equations, by putting all the Equation over to one lidc, and thereby making the whole equal to nothing; whereby also he determined the Number of Roots; which he shews are in Number, such as the Index of the highest Power in the Equation. 4. He discovers the true Construction of the Ab^ solute Number (the Homogencum Comparationis) in a Quadratick or Superiour Equation; (hewing it to be the Product of the continual Multiplication of all the Roots. 5. The same he doth also by the Co-efficients. 6. He (news the way to multiply the unknown Roots of an Equation according to any Proportion assigned, thereby freeing the Co-efficients from Fractions and Surds. 7. He (news how to reduce all adfected Quadraticks to simple Equations, and all adfected Cubicks to a Form easily solvable, by the means of destroying the second Term in such Equations. 8. He strews the Method (and a very good one 'tis) of solving all Adfected Quadraticks by completing the Square. 9. He mightily also improves the Exegesis Numerofa invented by Vieta. All these vast Improvements, and many more .(which to avoid Prolixity I omit) did Des-Cartes take from Harriot , without ever so much as naming him, and publish them as his own. ’Tft true, in his Geometry there are abundance of excellent things about the Accommodation of Algebra to Geometrical Propositions, and many very fine Geometrical Ejfeciicns and Constructions, but this

UG A JL I rhiS was not Harriot Business, who kepi himself j to pare Algebra only. As to which Dcs-Carttt .j scath added but one single Rule (and even that: w plainly deducible from Harriott's Principles)! over and above what is in Harriott ; and that is, 1 the Method of dissolving a Biquadratick Equaiij on, whose ad Term is wanting, into two Quaj draticks, by means of a Cubtck Equation ot a j Plain Root; and this after all, both Pom bell and Vieta had done before him. And thus leaving this French Plagiary, I come next to another of 4 >«r Country Algebrilts, Dr. Fell, who revised and altered a Piece of Algebra first published in High Dutch, A. D. 1659 at ostrich j and after Translated into English by Mr. Thomas Brandt**, and Printed A. D, 1668, and called, An Intro - dullion to Algebra In which Dr. Pell gives us a peculiar Method of his own for applying to Problems of divers lores; and introduced the way ot keeping a Register of the whole Process in the Margin. He Ihews us also there how to judge whether a Problem be fully determined or not ; which is by this Rule (' as Dr. iVallis interprets bun). If the Number of the Data, or things given in any Question, be (independent of each other) server than the things fought, the Question is not fully determined, but it capable of innumerable An • steers or Solutions . But if the Number of both Data and Quaisita be the same, then the Question is then determined to either some one, or to some certain Number of Solutions. And when the Data are more in Number than the Qu.cstta, so many as exceed are always superfluous, and sometimes, it may be, are contrary to, or inconsistent with others, and consequently render the thing impossible. Dr. Pell also, besides the former Characters, introduced this Mark © for Involution, and this uu for Evolution , as he calls it $ *. e. for Squaring, Cubing, &cc. of any Quantity, and fur ExtraEiing the Square, Cube, &c. Roots out of any Quantity. He makes also this Mark — to stand for Division , and Registers the several Steps ot the whole Process by the Numeral Figures in their order in the little Column in the middle; keeping an Account also in Symbols ot the several Operations in the Column towards the Left-hand, that so you may see how any Quantity or Equation in the large Column towards the Right-hand is produced. In which very good Method he is followed by bVard in his small Treatise of Algebra. Algebra is well enough divided into I. Numeral or Vulgar; which was that of the Ancients, and served only to find the Solution of Arithmetical Problems without any De-, monstration ; Such as those given us by Diepban - j *us, & c. l. Specious or New, called sometimes LogiSUca Speqiofa, and often Species alone; which since K‘ eta b^th been performed by the Letters of the Alphabet. And this way of Notation is very pleating to the Mind, assisting to the Imaginati. on > and easie to the Memory. This also is no wa ys limited, like the former Algebra to anyone certain kind of Problems, but serves equally for the Investigation and Demonstration of all Theorems j especially if to thole two you add the new Methods of 3. Fiuidms ; a large Account of which you will have under that Word. And lie several Operations of Algebra, such as Addition , -Substr-aHion , Multiplication , Division , Extradion of Boots, Frail ions , Equations, Lee. you will find Directions ixaw to perform under those several Words.

algeneb.c: ALGENEB, a six’d Star of the second Magnitude in the right side oiFerfeus, whole Longitude is 57 deg. 17 ntin. Latitude 30. 5. Right Ascension 44 deg. 1 5 win.

algol.c: ALGOL, or Medusas Head, a six’d Star of the third Magnitude, in the Constellation Perseus , whole Longitude is 51. 37. Latitude aa. a a. and Declination, 39. 39.

algorithm.c: ALGORITHM, sometimes called Logistic* Numeraiis, is the Sumtn of the Principal Rules of Numeral Computation; of which they commonly reckon Five, Numeration, Addition, Substrataa on, Multiplication and Division; to which aiay be added Extraliion of Roots,

algorism.c: ALGORISM, is the Practical Operation in the several Parts of Specious Arithmetics. Ot Algebra ; and sometimes the Word is used for the Practice of Common Arithmctick by the Ten Numeral Figures.

alidada.c: ALIDADA , the Label or Ruler which is moveable on the Centre of an Astrolabe Quadrant, (&c.. which carries the Sight. It is so case led by the Arabian Writers of Mathematicks, from whom we took and retain several Arabics Terms, as Azimuth, stnith , Nadir , Alma can* ter , 8cc.

alien.c: ALIEN, a Subject born in a Foreign Country, who (by our Common Law) is not capable to inherit l ends in England till Naturaliz’d by Act of Parliament.

alienation.c: ALIENATION, is (in Law) to make a thing another Man's, or to alter or put the Possession of Lands or other things from one Man to another ; and in some Cases a Alan hath power in himself to do so, without the Assent or Licence of any other, and in some not.

aliformesmusculi.c: ALIFORMES MUSCULI, Alares, Pterygoides , are Muscles arising from the Pterygoidc Bones (the Process of the Os Cuneiform*, partly with a Nervous beginning, and partly fleshy ; and ending in the Neck of the lower Jaw, and towards the Internal Seat of the Head.

aliformesprocesses.c: ALIFORMES PROCESSES, are the Prominences of the Os Cuneiforme, from the fore part; the same with the Pterygoides.

aliment.c: ALIMENT, is whatever serves to nourish, supply the Decays of, and to recruit an Animal or Vegetable Body.

alimony.c: ALIMONY, formerly signified Nourilhmenr or Maintenance, but in a Modern Legal Sence, it is that Portion or Allowance which a Married Woman sues for, upon any occasional Separation from her Husband, wherein site is not charged with Elopement or Adultery. This was recoverable in the Spiritual Court, but now only in Chancery.

aliquotpartofanumber.c: ALIQUOT PART of a Number, is such au one as will exactly measure it without any Remainder. But an

aliquantpart.c:
ALIQUANT PART, is that which cannot measure any Number exactly, but that some Remainder will be left. Thus 3 is an Aliquot part of 1 a, because being taken four tunes ie will

A L K ALL will just measure it; but Five is an Aliquant part of i L, for being taken twice it falls short, and when taken three times it exceeds ti.

alkahest.c: ALKAHEST ; one of the Canting Terms of the AlchymUts, by which they intend an Universal. that will dissolve all manner ot Bodies; and by which they pretend to. extract the Sulphur of Metals. Some Chemists have given this mighty Name to the Tincture, or Liquor of Flints, which is a Solution of them made (alter Calcination) by the means of Salt of Tartar ; and others tO the Liquor of Fixt Nitre, which is Nitre calcined and fixed by burning powdered Coals with it, and at lass run into a Dcliquium by being let in a cool Cellar, as Oyl of Tartar per Dcliquium is made. Van-Hdmont calls this Liquor sometimes Ignis Gehenna:: He pretends to be Master of it himself, and Mr. Boyle is inclin’d to believe him. Helmont faith, it would dissolve all Bodies, without leaving any Captip bbrtuum, and was as fit for a new Operation after it had dissolved one kind of Body as at first ; it would dissolve Metals, Marchasites, Stones, and even Glass itself when finely powder’d. Mis found, that the common Menflruums, such as Aqua Fortis, Spirit of Nitre, &c. when they have once dissolved any Metal, are rendered uncapable by it of any further service, having the Points or Edges of their Acids so broken, that they can hardly dissolve any more of the same, or any other Metal. Therefore this Immortal Ah kahest had in this respect a wonderful prehemincnce, if what they relate of it be true. And shew that something of this nature is possible, Mr. Boyle says, That he distilled a Spirit from Verdigrealc, which would serve more than once as a Menstruum to dissolve Bodies, or to draw Tinctures, and being drawn off was ready for the same Operation anew.

alkalisatespiritofwine.c: ALKALIS ATE Spit ut OF WINE; so Mr. Boyle calls a Spirit of that Liquor distilled from Salt of Tartar, or Tartar calcined to Whiteness: And by so drawing off' Spirit of Wine from that Salt, yOu may get easily a pure and rich dephlegmated Spirit <vi%. one that shall burn all away, and sire Gunpowder) after this manner. Put about an Inch thick of Tartar ^asci ned white, into a Glass as long and slender as you can procure, and then put upon it Spirit of Wine that hath been once rectify vi, to a Finger’s height above the Tartar, and fitting on a Head, draw the Spirit off in a very gentle Heat; or at least, so much of it as you conclude or find will come pure, and it will answer your Expectation ac the first Distillation. The Tartar being dried and new calcined will serve again for a new Operation. If you cannot procure Tartar, Quick-limc or the Salt of Pot-ashes will do tolerably well. alkali.c: ALKALI. A Chymical Word signifying the hxt Salt of any Plant ; and is so called, because rise Herb called Kali, which is a kind of Scab.'ite, Glass-tvort, or Salt-veort, yields such a Salt to a great (Quantity. This Fixt Salt of Plants (•which is made by burning the Plant, making a Lixivium or Lee of its Assies; and after filtrating the Lee, evaporating the Moisture over a gentle Heat, that the Fixt Salt may remain at the bottom of the Vessel) being rendred very Porous by the Fire’s passing so often through it in its Calcination, and it may be fixing there some of its Essential Salt: And because very many of the Fiery Particles do also stick in thole Pores, makes a very great Ebullition or effervescence when any Acid Liquor is mingled with it. and from thence all Bodies that do, or are supposed to ferment with Acids, are now always called Alkalies on Alkalis ate Bodies ; net because they must always contain any Hidden Alkali in them ; which some Chymists assert as necessary to the Cause of Fermentation ; but because they are of the Nature of Alkalies themselves, and have their Pores naturally so formed, in such a Proportion, as that they are fitted to be penenated and put into a violent Motion by the Points of the Acid poured upon them. These fixt Salts of Plants arc called Fixt Alkalies ; but the Volatile Salts of Vegetables, because they will ferment with Acids, arc called Volatile Alkalies. .

alkermes.c: ALKERMES, in Pharmacy, is a Confection described in the Dispensatory, and so d in the Shops, and so called from the Acabick Particle Al and formes, which arc Red or Scarlet Grains, the chief Ingredient in the Confection.

allanloisorallantoides.c: ALLAN l’OIS or ALLANTOIDES, is the Vrinary Tunic placed betwixt the Amnion and the Cborion, which by the Navel and Drachus , (or Passage by which the Urine is Conveyed from the Infant in the Womb) receives the Urine that comes out of the Bladder: It’s called likewise Farciminalis, because that in many Brutes it’s of the shape of a Gut-pudding, but in Man and some other few Animals, it is round, and like the thin soft Skin which wrappeth the Child in the Womb. The Ingenious and Accurate Dr. Bieh. Hale of Trin. Coll. in Oxford, in Phil. Trans ael. N. 271, hath obliged the World with a more perfect Discovery of the Human Allantois, and assigned the Reasons why those who believed its Existence had not before fully found it out; giving also an Answer ro the Objections of those who even still deny its Reality.

allegation.c: ALLEGATION, is the Citation or Quotation of any Authority, Book, &e. to make good any Point or Assertion.

allegory.c: ALLEGORY, is a Figure in Rlietorick, consisting of one continued Metaphor, carried on through the whole Discourse.

allegiantia.c: ALLEGIANTIA, is the natural and sworn Allegiance or Legal Obedience which every Subject bears to his Prince.

allegiare.c: ALLEGIARE, is to justifie and clear himself by course of Law, of the Crime objected to him.

allemande.c: ALLEMANDE, is a kind of grave solemn Mulick, where the Measure is full and the Movement slow.

alliance.c: ALLIANCE, properly is a Connection of two Persons or two Families together by Marriage ; but 'tis often extended in a larger Sense, to signifie the Leagues, Unions and Treaties made between Princes, &c.

alligation.c:
ALLIGATION, is a Rule in Arithmetick (To called from the Numbers being bound or connected together by Circular Lines) relating to the mixture of Merchandices, as Corn, Wine, Metals, Medicines, Ac. one with another; and to the Proportion of the Ingredients in any Quantity of, and the Price of such a Mixture. ’Tis distinguished

ALL ALL stinguifhed into two kinds, vi%. Alligation Medial and Alternate, Alligation Medial teaches how to find a Mean in the Price, Quantity, or Quality between the Extreams; and all Cafes in it may be solved by these Propositions and Rules. 1. Having the Quantities of the Ingredients, and the particular Prices, to find the Price or Value of some part of the Mixture. Rule, Multiply the Ingredients severally by their own Prices, and divide the Summ of thole Products by the Summ of the Ingredients, and the Quotient answers the Question. 2. Having the particular Prices of the Ingredients, and the Summ paid or received for a Mixture bought or sold, to find what Quantity of each was bought or sold. Rule, Divide the Summ paid or received for the Mixture bought or sold, by the Summ of the ■particular Prices, the Quotient gives what was required. 3 - Knowing the Ingredients of a Mixture, to augment or diminish the Mixture proportionally. Rule. Sum up the Ingredients, then say, As that Summ is to the Augmentation or Diminution, so is the Quantity of each Parcel of the Mixture, to the Quantity of the Mixture desired. 4. Knowing the Nature, Quality or Fineness of the several Ingredients of a Mixture, to find the resulting Temperament or Fineness of the whole. Risse. Place the several Quantities of the Mix ture in Rows, against which place orderly their several Qualities of Fineness, and multiply each Quantity by its own Quality or Degree of Fineness, then as the Summ of all the Quantities is to the Products of all the Quantities, so is Unity to the Quality or Fineness of Mixture. Example. There are melted and mixed together two kinds of Silver, one worth 5 s. and the other worth 4 s. an Ounce, and there were 4 Ounces of the former and 8 of the latter ; what is the value of an Ounce of the Mixture ? Oun. s, t. d. Silver 4 + 5 =i° ia: 52 :; 1 = t !(=4 4 - 1 + 4=3 12 51 5. Knowing the Quantities of a Mixture, to find the particular Quantities of any Ingredient in any part of the Mixture. If the Mixture be compounded of but two things, then lay, As the Total of the Ingredients tn the Composition is to the part of the Mixture proposed, so is the Quantity of the Ingredient proposed in the whole Composition, to the Quantj ry of the Ingredient in the Part desired. Put if the Mixture be decompounded, then you must repeat your Work upon every Mix6. Knowing the Total of a Mixture, with the dotal Value, and tjie Values of the several InSredients mixed, to find the several Quantities though unequally. 1 ti% ^“hiply the Total of the Mixture by the Vi Value » subtract the Product from the Total I4 j ue, and the Remainder is the first Dividend: v , j a r ke the laid least Value from the greatest valued ingredient, and the Remainder is the first Divisor. The Quotient of this Division Ihews the Quantity of the highest priz’d Ingredient, the either is the Complement to the whole: And when more Ingredients than two are in the Composition, the Divisors are the several Remains of the least Value taken from the other. The Dividends are the Remains left upon the Divisions till o remain there; which will be one sort of the number of Ingredients, and this defective Ingredient is to be supplied as a Complement; and in Division no more must be taken in every Quotient, than that there may remain enough for the other Divisors, and the last co leave nothing remaining. 2. Alligation Alternate, shews the due proportion of every Ingredient entring the Mixture, and counter-changes the places of such Excesses or Differences as fall out between the Mean Price and the Extreams, ascribing it to the greater Extream which proceeds from the Lester, and the contrary. Rtile 1. Let every greater Extrcam be linked with one lesser. 2. When either of the Extreams be single, and the other Extreams be plural, the single Extream must be linked to all the rest. 3. If both greater and lesser Extreams are nor single, then they may be linked so diversly, that sundry Differences may be taken, and Diversities of Answers to the Question, yet all true : But it one of the Extreams be single, there can be but one Answer. 4. The Numbers being linked, take the Difference of each Number from the Mean or Common Price, and place this Difference against the Number it is linked co alternately. 5. Every Number linked with more than one, must have all the Differences of the Numbers it is linked to let against it. 6. Those Differences resolve the Question, when the Price of every of the Ingredients is given without their Quantities, and the Demand be to mix them so as to fell a certain Quantity at a mean rate. 7. But when the Quantity of one, with the Price of all the Ingredients is given, and the Demand is to know the Quantities of the other Ingredients, then the Rule of Three is to be used. 8. And when the Price of every Ingredient is given, without any of their Quantities, and the Demand be to make up a certain Quantity to be sold at a mean Rare, then all the Differences added together shall be the first Number in the Rule of Three ; the whole Quantity to be mixed shall be the 2d. Number; and each Difference apart the several third Numbers and so many forts mix’d, so many Operations of the Rule of Three. 9. A Question may be so propounded, as both sorts of Alligation is needful to the Resolution. Example. Suppose a Mixture of Wine of 1 19 Quarts he required , that muR be made up of these several Prices , 7 d. 8 d, 14 d. and 15 d. so as the whole may be afforded at 12d. per Quart. allioth.c: ALLIOTH, the Name of a Star in the Tail of the great Bear , whose Observation is much used at Sea. The Elevation of the Pole or the Latitude may thus be easily found by this Star. Observe when Allioth comes to the Meridian under the Pole, then take the Height of the PoleStar with a Quadrant, and out of that substract 2 °. 2 ;'. the Distance of the Pole-Star from the Pole , the Remainder is the Pole's Height, or the Latitude.

alliteration.c: ALLITERATION (a Figure in Rhetorick) is a repeating and playing on the same Letter.

allocationefacienda.c: ALLOCATIONE FACIENDA, is a Writ directed to the Lord Treasurer and Barons of the Exchequer, upon complaint of some Accountant, commanding them to allow him such Summs as he hath by vertue of his Office lawfully and reasonably expended.

allocation.c: ALLOCATION, in Law, is an Allowance made upon an Accompc.

allodiallands.c: ALLODIAL Lands , are those, for which no Rents, Fines, nor Services are due. Such as Proe land.

allodium.c: ALLODIUM, a Law-term, signifying, every Man’s own Land, &c. which he possesseth meerly in his own Right, without acknowledgment of any Services, or payment of any Rent to another, which is a Property in the highest degree.

alloeticks.c: ALLOETICKS, are Medicines consisting chiefly of Aloes.

allogotrophy.c: ALLOGOTROPHY, with some Writers, is a Disproportionate Nutrition of the Body; when one part (as in the Rickets) is nourished more than the other.

alloy.c: ALLOY, is the Proportion of a Baser Metal mingled with a Finer or Purer; as the Quantity of Copper that is mingled with Gold to make it of a due hardness to be coined into Money, is called its Alloy : And Gold that hath more of this than it ought to have, is said to be of a Courser or Greater Alloy. The Proportion of Alloy for Gold used in our Mints is about a 12 th part.

almacanters.c: ALMACANTERS, an Arahick. word signifying the lame with Parallels of Altitude on the Globe’. Which lee. Some write it Almicantcrahs , and Others Ahnacantcrahs. ALMACANTERS SI AFF, is an Instrument usually made of Pear-Tree or Box, with an Arch only of 15 degrees, to take Observations of the Sun, about the times of its Rising and Setting, in order to find the Amplitude , and consequently the Variation, of the Compass.

almondsofthethroatorthetonsilhe.h: ALMONDS of the Throat or the Tonsilhe
almondsofthethroatorthetonsilhe.c: ALMONDS of the Throat or the Tonsilhe ; a Gland ulous Substance representing two Kernels placed on each side of the Uvula, at the Root of the Tongue. They arc covered with the common Tunic of the Mouth, and have Veins and Arteries from the Carotidcs and Jugulars: They arc of a lax and spongy Substance, having leveral Sinus's within them, in which they contain rite I .iqaior of the Saliva, which they receive from the Brain, and by dispersing it to the Larynx t Jaws, Tongue, and Oesophagus , do moisten and lubricate those Parts when these are swelled and inflamed by a Cold, &c. they very much straiten the Pa stage of the Throat, and render Swallowing painful and difficult, and help to make what we call a fore Throat, and as the Country People say, the coming down of the Almonds of the Ears.

almucanterahs.c: ALMUCANTERAHS, the same with Almacanters : Which see.

alopecy.c: ALOPECY, is a shedding of the Hair, occasioned by the Pox, or otherwise: So called from a Fox dhaon^, whose Urine is said to make places bald, and barren for a Year, as the Scholiast on Callimachus observes; or from a Disease peculiar to a Fox. It is called likewise opittoif, from the Figure, because that the parts smooth and destitute of Hair, look winding like a Serpent, in Greek c<pt <: It's common to both these Distempers that the Hair fall of Areatim, i. e. by shedding, whence in general this Disease is called Area. Blanchard.

alpheta.c: ALPHETA, the Name of a Star : See Lueida Corona.

alphus.c: ALPHUS, isa CuteaneousDistemper in which the Skin is rough, and looks here and there as if there were Drops of a white colour upon it : Some call it Morphew ; it differs from the Leuce, in that it penetrates not so deep as the Leuce doth.

alramech.c: ALRAMECH, a Star’s Arabics Name, which is the same with Arllurus.

alterage.c: ALTERAGE, or ALd ARAGIUM, is a word which includes not only the Offerings made upon the Altar, but also all the Profit that arises to the Priest by reason of the Altar,

alteration.c: ALTERATION, is, in a Physical Sense, that Motion by which a Body is varied or changed in some Circumstances from what it really was before, though as to Sense its Nature and Bulk appear to continue still the same; so that it consists in the Bodies acquiring or losing such Qualities, as whether present or absent, do not essentially change the Subject : And herein it differs from Generation and Corruption, which Terms express the Acquisition or Loss of the Essential Qualities of any Body. Or otherwise,

ALTERATION, is an Accidental and Partial Change made in any Body, without proceeding so far as to make the Subject be quite unknown, or to take a new Name or Denomination upon it: Or it may be called the Acquisition or Loss of such Qualities as are not Essential to the Form of any Body.

alteringremedies.c: ALTERING REMEDIES ; such Medicines as serve to purify and restore the due Mixture of the Blood, and other circulating Humours.

alternateproportion.c: ALTERNATE PROPORTION: See the word Proportion, N". 8.

alternbase.c: AIT ERN BASE, a Term in Trigonometry, distinguished from the True Base , thus; In Oblique Triangles the Tute Base is always either the Sum of the Sides, (and then the Difference of the Sides is called the Ahem Base) or the True Base is the Difference, and then the 'morn of the Sides is called the AI tern Base. ALTERA L T ALT

alternation.c: ALTERNATION, is a word u!cd by Ox.lPal- \ /wand others for the different Changes or Alterations of: Order in an) Number of things proposed. Or this that Learned Mathematician hath a peculiar Discourse at the end of his Algebra. This Alternation is easily found, by only continual Multiplication of all the Numbers, beginning at Unic V’ i Thus if it were required to know how many^ Changes can be rung on six Bells, you need only write down i, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and then multiply all those Numbers continually one into another, and the last Product gives the Number of I Changes, which is 720 Changes.

altimetry.c: ALTIMETRY, the Art of taking and measuring of Heights, whether Accessible or Inaccessible. See Altitudes or Heights,

altitudeofthepole.c: ALL ITUDE of the Pole: See Elevation of the Pole.

altitudeofmotion.c: ALTITUDE of MOTION, is a Term used by Dr. TVallts in his Mcchanicks for the Measure of any Motion estimated according to the Line of Direction of the moving Force.

altitudesorheightsofplacesperpendicularl.h: ALTITUDES or Heights of Places perpendicularly above the Horizon

Having Resisted the Globe, and fitted the Quadrant, bring ir to cut the True East Point, and then turn the Globe till the Sun’s Place in the Ecliptick cut the graduated Edge of the Quadrant, for then that place will shew the Altitude, and the Index, the Hour. ALTO & BASSO, for in Alto, (3 in Basso) in Law signifies the Absolute Submission of all Differences, small and great, high and low, to a Judge or Arbitrator.

aludels.c: ALUDELS, are Pots used by the Chymists in Sublimations: They are without Bottoms, and are fitted into one another as many as thera is occasion: At the Bottom (in the Furnace} there is a Pot holding the Matter to be sublimed ; and at the fop there is a Head to receive the Flowers that full tem up thither. This is the Figure of them. The Head: 2, 3, Three Aktdelsi The Pot holding the Matter to be sublimed. The Fire-place. The Stopple of the Fire-place.

alvearium.c: ALVEARIUM, is the Cavity of the inward Ear, near the Passage which conveys the Sound: where that yellow and bitter cxcrementitious Stuff is bred, called Ear-Wax.

amain.c: AMAIN ; a word used at Sea when a Man of War giveth Defiance to another Ship, or biddeth her strike herTopfaiJs or yield ; for to bid a Ship strike Amain, is to order her to let fall her Topsails.

amalgamate.c:
AMALGAMATE, a Chymical Term signifying the mixing Quicksilver with some melted Metal : The Design of which is either to render the Metal fit to be extended on some Works, as in Gilding, ( 3 c. or else to reduce the Metal into a very subtile Powder. The Amalgama of Gold is thus made ; Take a Dram of the Reguleof Gold, beat it into very thin little Plates, which heat in a Crucible Red hot in a strong Fire, then pour on it an Ounce of pure Quicksilver ; stir the Matter with an Iron Rod, aud when you find it beginning to raise a Fume, which will soon happen, cast it into an Earthen Pan filled with Water j it will co-ag ulate and become tractable. Waff. it often to take away its Blackness, and pressing from it with your Fingers and in a Linen Cloth, that Mercury that remains un united with the Gold. The Gold will retain about thrice its weight of the Mercury. If you would reduce the Gold into Powder, put this Amalgam into a Crucible over a gentle Fire, and the Mercury will evaporate into the Air, and leave the Gold at the bottom in an Impalpable Powder, which you may melt into its first Form again; and if it should retain any Blackness from the Mercury , Oyl of Tartar per Dehquium will fetch it off. For Experiment fake, you may majae a Lumi - nous Amalgama after this manner. Put into a long Vial 10 Grains of the Phosphorus made from Urine, and pour on it two Drams of Oyl of Afpike : The Glass must be large enough for two 36s at least to remain empty. Heat it a little with a Candle and the phosphorus will »

AME A M O —r r—- - --—--- will dissolve with an Ebullition: Whilst this Dissolution is making, pour into it half a Dram of pure Quicksilver, Inaking the Glass that the Matter may be stirred and mixed. You will have an Amalgam;i which will appear all of a fire in the Dark ; but it must, like the Phosphorus , be kept close stopt from Air; else it will be soon spoil’d. if the Amalgam bcdesign'd to be so hard, as to be fit to be powdred, you must take 3 parts of the Metal and 2 of Mercury ; but if you would have it so soft as to spread, you must use 3 parts of Mercury to one of the other Metal.

amanses.c: AMANSES, a Barbarous Factitious Word which some of the Canting Chymists use for counterfeit Gems and precious Stones. AMAUROS 1 S, is a dimness of Sight, whether the Object be placed near or ac distance; but so that no external fault appear in the Eye, if you inspect it never so narrowly ; the Defect consists in the Obstruction of the Optic Nerve; It is called also Gutta Serena, Blanchard.

ambages.c: AMBAGES, an Idle Circumlocution, or vain connecting together of far fetcht Words or Sayings, remote from the true purpose of the Speaker. AM BE, is a superficial jutting out ot the Bones: Also a Chyrurgeons Instrument, with Which dif-jointed Bones are set again.

ambidexter.c: AMBIDEXTER (in Law) signifies, that Juror or Embraceor that takes Money of both Parties for giving of his Verdict, for which he forfeits ten times as much as he taketh. And ordinarily Ambidexter denotes that Man that can equally use both his Hards.

ambient.c: AMBIENT, encompassing round about. Thus the Bodies which happen to be placed round any other Body are called the Ambient, and often the C 'ircum-Ambient Bodies; and the whole Body of the Air, because it encompasses all things on the Face of the Earth, is often by Physical Writers called by Way of eminence, The Ambient.

ambit.c: AMBIT, of any Figure in Geometry, is the Perimeter, Circumference, or Sumrn of all the Bounding or Encompassing Lines that include it.

ambligonial.c: AMBLIGONIAL, in Geometry, signifies Obtujangular, or that the sides of any Plane Figure make an Obtuse Angle one with another. Thus an Ambligonial Triangle is that which hath one Obtuse Angle.

amblyopia.c: AMBLTOPIA, is a dulness or dimness of Sight when the Object is not clearly difeern'd at what distance soever placed, and proceeds from an imperfect Obstruction of thcOptick Nerves, a light Suffusion, want of Spirits, or grossness of the lame, <j?c. Some reckon 4 kinds of Ambliopia, viz. Myopia, Presbytia, Ny da so pi a, and Atnaurofis Which lee under thole Words. Blanchard.

amblyotickmedicines.c: AMBLOTICK Medicines, are such as cause Abortion.

ambuscade.c: AMBUSCADE, a Place where Soldiers hide themselves to surprise the Enemy.

amendment.c: AMENDMENT (a Common-Law Term) sign fy> r f>. the Correction of an Error committed inn Process, and espied before Judgment, but m;'.v !vi amended by the Justices after Judgment; - and if there be Error in giving Judgment, they y not amend it, but the Party is to put in his \Vru of Error.

amercement.c: AMERCEMENT (a Term in Law) is a Peal; . assclVd by the Peers, or Equals of the Par. cy acictced, for an Offence done.

amercementroyal.c: AMERCEMENT ROYAL, is when a Sheriff. Coroner, or other such Officer of the King is time reed by the Justices for abuse in his Office. Blunt makes this Difference between Amercements and Fines : That the latter as taken for Punishments, are Punishments certain, which grow expressly from some Statute ; and Amercements are arbitrarily imposed by Ajfeerors <

amethist.c: AMETHIST, in Heraldry, is the Term for the Purple Colour in the Coat of a Ncble-man; which in all Gentlemcns Escutcheons below that Degree is called Purpure, and in those of Sovereign Princes Mercury.

amitterelegemterr.c: AM1TTERE LEGEM TERRÆ.aLaw Term, signifying, to sole the Liberty ot Swearing in any Court, to become infamous; the Punishment of a Champion overcome or yielding in a Fight, or in Bated, and the Jurors found guilty in a Writ of Ataivt, and of a Person outlawed.

amnesty.c: AMNESTY, is an Act of Oblivion ; such as was granted at King Charles' s Restauration.

amnionoramnios.c: AMNION or AMNIOS, is the innermost Membrane with which the Foetus in the Womb is most immediately covered, and with which the rest of the Sccundincs, the Choi ton, and Allantcis is ejected after the Birth; it is whiter and thinner than the Chorion. It contains not only the Foetus, but the Nutritious Humour, whence the Foetus by the Mouth and Throat sucks its Nourishment; It is outwardly cloathed with the Urinary Membrane, and the Chorion, which sometimes sticks so close to one another, that they can scarce be separated: Though it is not knit to the Chorion in any place lave where the Umbilical Vessels pass through them both, into the Placenta. It hath Vessels from the fatnc Origin as the Chorion, Before the Ovum is impregnated this Membrane contains a Limpid Liquor, out of which, after Impregnation, the Embryo is formed. In it (says Gibson ) resides the PJastick Power, and the Matter also out of which the first Lineamants of the Embryo are drawn ; but because its Liquor is so very little, there Transudes through this Membrane the Amnion, a part of that Nutritious Albugineous Humour which is contained in the Chorion, which it had imbibed out of the Uterus and by the JuxtaPosition or Addition of Its Humour to undiscernible Rudiments of the Embryo, it receives its encrcasc. But though the Amnion have its assilitional Nutritious Liquor at first only by Transudarion, yet when the Umbilical Vessels and the Placenta are formed, it receives it after another manner ; for then its Liquor being separated from she Mother's Arteries by the Placenta, and imbibed by the Umbilical Vein of the Foetus, it passes directly to its Heart, from whence being driven out by the Aorta, it is sent forth again, in good part, by the Umbilical Arteries, out of whose Cavities, being plentifully dispersed through the Amnion it issues into its Cavity; just as J vices which are far more gross and viscid than this, do sometimes critically, and often on taking a Purge, oure into the Intestines out of the small Mouths of the Arteries: Indeed here the Intervention of the Glands assists this Matter ; but ‘tis hoped some curious Person one time or other will discover, that there are such also in the Amnion.

amortise.c:
AMORTISE (a Term in Law) is to alien Land or Tenements to any Corporation, Guild cf

AMP ANA or Fraternity, and their Successors, which cannot be done without Licence of the King, and the Lord of the Mannor.

ampelite.c: AMPELITE (in Agriculture) is a kind of Black or Bituminous Earth, used about Vines, to make them thrive the better.

amphibology.c: AMPHIBOLOGY, a Grammatical Figure, when our Expressions seem to look one way, and are intended another. AMPH 1 BLESTROIDES, or the Tunica. Retintl or Retiformis of the Eye, is a loft, white and slimy Substance, which is so named, because that Being thrown in the Water, it resembles a Nett; it shoots from the very Center of the Optick Nerve, and consists of the Medullar Substance of ? c > and expanding it self over the Vitreous Humour, is extended as far as the LigamentumCiliare or the Ligaments of the Eye lids: This Tunic, in that tt is whitish, and of a Marrowy Substance, seems to proceed from the veiy Marrowy and Fibrous Substance of the Optick Nerve, so that it is as it were an Expansion of Nervous Fibres, which are there gathered, into one Bundle, into a Contexture made like a Net; and indeed if the whole Eye were taken for a Flower, growing as it were to the Brain by the Stalk of the Optick Nerve, the Tunica Retina would be the very Flower it self, and the two other Tunicles, the Sclerotica and Chordaes, be only in the nature of a Stem. This Tunick seems to be the Principal Organ of Sight, and receives the visible Species within the Bed of the Eye much after the lame manner as a whited Wall or a piece of White Paper in a darkened Chamber, receives and represents the visible Species which are int remitted through a little hole. See Camera Obfcura.

amphibrachys.c: AMPHIBRACHYS, is the Foot of a Latin Verse consisting of three Syllables, where the two extreams are short, and the middle long, as Amare.

amphibranchia.c: AMPHIBRANCHIA, are places about the Glandules in the Jaws, which moisten the Afpera Arteria and Stomach. I

amphibious.c: AMPHIBIOUS, is used for an Animal that ' ves Both on Land and in the Water, as an Oter > Beaver, &c. AMPHlMACER, is the Foot of a Latin Verse, ^nlisting of three Syllables ; the two extreams 0n S and the middle short as Caftitas, AMPHIDÆUM, with some Writers is the summit or Top of the Mouth of the Womb. ■°‘an chard.

amphiprostyle.c: AMPHIPROSTYLE, a Term in Architecture so 1 of Temple of the Ancients, which had ur Columns in the Front, and as many in the Fa ce behind.

ampliation.c: AMPLIATION (in Law) signifies, a deferring of Judgment, till the Cause be further examined.

amplification.c: AMPLIFICATION ('in Rhetorick) is a Figurative Speech aggravating a Crime, enlarging in praise of an’other, or insisting upon a Relation, (Fc.

amputation.c: AMPUTATION, is the Surgeon’s Term for the cutting off any Member of the Body.

amulet.c: AMULET, any thing that is hung about the Neck or any part of the Body, supposed to be good against Witchcraft or Diseases. These were called anciently Prœbia, Apotropcca , Phylaileria, Amynteria, Alexiteria, and Alcxipharmaca.

amunition.c: AMUNITION, in the general, is all forts of Warlike Stores and Provisions; especially Powder and Ball.

amunitionbread.c: AMUNITION BREAD, in an Army, is that which is provided for and distributed to the Soldiers.

amy.c: AMY (is a Law Term) signifying the next to be trusted for an Q r phan c>r Infant.

amygdalate.c: AMYGDALATE, in Pharmacy, is an Artificial Milk, or Emulsion made of blanched Almonds,

ana.c: ANA, a kind of Barbarous Word used amongst the Writers of Pharmacy, and signifies, that an equal Quantity of those Ingredients With which it is connected is taken for the Composition of any Medicine.

anabibazon.c: ANABIBAZON, the Dragons Head, or the Northern Node of the Moon, where she passes from South to North Latitude, is sometimes so called.

anabrochismus.c: ANABROCHISMUS, is a way of drawing out the inverted pricking Hairs of the Eye-lids, by means of a Thread of fine Silk in the Eye of a Needle, which when you have doubled, you put the Hair through, and so draw it out.

anabrosis.c: ANABROSIS, is a consuming or wasting of any part of the Body by sharp Humours. ANAANA ANA

anacamptick.c: ANACAMPTICK, signifies Reflecting ; Vis frequently used in reference to Echoes, which are Sounds produced Anacamptically or by Reflection : And therefore Ana camp ticks is by some taken for Catoptricks.

anacatharsis.c: ANACATHARSIS, is a Medicine that discharges Nature by some ot the upper parts; as any thing that provokes to vomit, to Sneezing, to Salivation, Q$c. in which last Sense Hippocrates used the word, as Galen faith.

anacathartickmedicines.c: ANACATHARTICK. MEDICINES, are such as cause Vomiting.

anacephaleosis.c: ANACEPHALEOSIS, is a brief Summary or Recapitulation of the Heads of any Matter spoken or delivered in Writing.

anachronism.c: ANACHRONISM, an Error in Chronology, an undue Connexion of Time, or a false Chro. nicling.

anaclaticks.c: ANACLATICKS, a part of Opticks which treats of all sorts of Refractions, and is the same with Dioptrics.

anacollema.c: ANACOLLEMA, is a kind of Liniment or dry Medicine, to be apply'd to the Forehead or Nose in Diseases of the Eyes, or to stop Bleeding; also a Medicine which will breed Flesh and conglutinate the Parts.

anacreonticsverse.c: ANACREONTICS VERSE, is a kind of Verse consisting of seven Syllables, without being tied to any certain Law of Quantity ; so called from its Author Anacreon, a Lyrics Poet.

anadiplosis.c: ANADIPLOSIS (a Figure in Rlsetorick ) when one Verse begins with the same word the last ended with. ’Tis also sometimes used in Medicine, for the Reduplication of the Paroxysms or Fits of Fevers ; and in this Sense ’tis called by some Writers Epanadiplosis.

anadosis.c: ANADOSIS, is sometimes used for whatever rends upwards in the Body, as a Vomit, G?r, but most usually for the Distribution of the Chyle through the proper Vessels.

anaglyphickart.c: ANAGLYPHICK ART, is the Art of Carving, Engraving, or Embossing.

anagogical.c: ANAGOGICAL, the same with Mysterious, or which hath an elevated, raised, uncommon Signification, or which raises the Mind up to Divine Contemplations.

anagram.c: ANAGRAM, is the Transposition of the Letters of any one’s Name, Title, &c. in order to make out from thence something to the Honour of the Person. Thus Galen by Transposition is Angel, &c.

AN ALE. P TICKS, are Medicines which cherish and renew the Strength ; it signifies also a part pf Hygicina, or the Art of preserving Health, whereby weak persons are recovered.

analogy.c: ANALOGY, in Matliematicks, is the Comparison of le ver al Ratio's together, much the same with Proportion : Which lee. And ’tis frequently used in Common Discourse for the word Proportion.

analogism.c: ANALOGISM ( in Logick) a forcible Argument, from the Cause to the Effect, implying an unanswerable Necessity.

analysis.c: ANALYSIS, a Resolution of any thing into its Component Principles: Thus a Chymist is said to Analyse Bodies when he ditlolves them by the Eire, and endeavours to find out their Constituent Parts: And Algebra is sometimes called the Analytics Art , because it teaches us to solve Questions and to demonstrate Theorems, by enquiring into the Bottom, into the Fundamental Constitution and Nature of the thing ; which is, as it Were resolved into its Parts, taken all to pieces, ind then put together again, that so we may fee into the Reason and Nature of it. And in this Sense Analytical Demonstrations are opposed to Synthetical ones: Winch see. The Ancients had some knowledge of this Art, but kept it concealed ; whose Invention Theo ascribes to Plato, and he defined it (according as Viet a renders it) AJfumpti Quastti tanquam conccjji, per confcquentia ad serum concejjum ; a taking of that as granted, or confessed which is enquired after, and thence goln 8 back by Consequences to what is confessedly true. Sc

analytick.c: ANALYTICK, in Logick, is a part of that ienee teaching to decline and construe Reason, a s Grammar doth words. Our famous Butitr makes his Impertinent Heroe and Scholar IIu4‘bras to be profoundly sit tell‘d in Analytick.

Such Verses ave called, ANAP/F.STICK VERSES; they are com- •non'y xif e d m T rit g c j; es , where are three Feet '"'nich are used in all parts of the Vcrlc indisserently . as 1 Castes (cquitur mt!a paupertas, I iti,’que potens reg nat Adulter. I ANAPHORA (a Figure in Rhetoric!?} is the Repetition of the same sound in the beginning of several Sentences or Verses. ANAPLEROT 1 CK MEDICINES, are such as help ro fill Ulcers with FJelli.

anarchy.c: ANARCHY, want of all Government in z Nation where there is no Supreme Authority lodged in either Prince or Rulers; but the People live without any Rule or Government at all-, and all things are in the utmost Confusion.

anasarcha.c: ANASARCHA, is a white, soft, yielding Tumour of the whole outward Body, or of some of its parts,which dents in by compressing the Flesh; it is caused by the Blood upon a double account; first, When it doth not rightly sanguify or assimilate the Chyle ; and again, when it is not rightly accended in the Lungs; the Blood thus perverted, pours forth the Scrum ar the Extremities of the Arteries in greater quantities than it can receive and reduce by the Veins and Lympheducts; or expel! by the Veins and Pores, and other passages that send it forth. If the Humours be too viscous it is called Lcucopblegmatia. Blanchard.

anastomatique.c: ANASTOMATIQUE ( Medicines ) are such as open and dilate the Orifices of the Vessels, and by that means help to make the Blood circulate freely, and pass easily out of the Arteries into the Veins.

anastomosis.c: ANASTOMOSIS, is an Esiluxion of the Blood, the Lympha or Chyle, at the meeting of Vessels that close not narrowly .- It is also taken for the mutual opening of Veins and Arteries into one another.

anatocism.c: ANATOCISM, is the Annual Iticrease or Interest of Money, whether Simple or Compound, And under it, they also comprehend the Validation of Annuities. See Interest.

anatomy.c: ANATOMY, is an Artificial Dissection of an Animal, especially Man, whereby the Parts are severally discovered and explained, for the use. of Phylick and Natural Philosophy ; and he that is skilful in this Art is called an Anatomist.

anchile.c: ANCHILE, is the back part of the Knee ; also the Contraction of a Joint, especially of the Ham.

anchor.c:
ANCHOR, cf a Ship, is a thing as well known as the Ship it felt, and also its use; but the Terms of Art used at Sea about its several Parts, Kinds and Uses are as followeth. The Parts of an Anchor are, (1.) The Ring, into which the Cable is fastened, (a) The Beam or Shank, which is the longest part of the Anchor. ( 3 .) The Ann, which is that which runs down into the Ground ; at the end of which is, (4.} The Elouly or Flu fe, by some called the Palm, being that broad and pecked part, with its Barbs like an Arrow-head , which fastens into the Ground. (5.) The Stocf, a piece of Wood fastened unto the Ream near the Ring, serving to' guide the Fluke, (0 that it may fall right ar.d six in the Ground. There are three finds ot Anchors, the Kedgcr, the Grapnel, and the Stream anchor: (Waich Jes under those Wordsi) Hie Anchors aboard a Mauds War are, the Fir it, Second and Third Anchors ; and two of Which being always carried a: the Bore of the Ship are therefore called .the First and Second Bovoyer : The other, which is the largest of all, is called the Sheet Anchor , and is these utmost Refuge when in a great Stress of Weather, they art forced to Ride on a Lee-Shore.

A N E When the Cable is perpendicular between the ^ star vie and the Anchor, the Anchor is then laid to i be a-pee.f When the Anchor hangs right up and down by the Ships side its said to be a Cocl^-Bcll upon the Ships coming to an Anchor. To put an Anchor down into the Sea in order to make the Ship Pfle, is called letting fall or dropping the Anchor. They lay an Anchor is soul, when by the turning about of the Ship the Cable is hitched about the Plus. An Anchor is said to come home, when it cannot hold the Ship, but that she drives away by the Violence of the Wind or Tide. To Shooc an Anchor, is, to put Boards fitted and formed for that purpose on upon the Flukes that the Anchor may the better hold in loft Ground. The Shank of an Anchor is to be 3 times the length of one of its Flukes; and a Ship of 500 Tun hath her Sheet Anchor of 2000 Weight; and so proportionably for others smaller or greater.

anchoring.c: ANCHORING, or Anchorage, is Ground fitting to hold a Ship’s Anchor, that so she may ride it out safely The belt Anchoring Ground is stiff Clay or hard Sand ; and the belt Riding at an Anchor is when a Ship is Landlockt and out of the Tide.

anchorage.c: ANCHORAGE (in Law) is a Duty taken of Ships for the Pool of the Haven where they cast Anchor; for no Man can let any Anchor fall on the King’s Ground in any Port, without paying for it to the King s Officer appointed by Patent.

anchylops.c: ANCHYLOPS , the same with Ægylops Which see.

ancient.c: ANCIENT, is the Flag or Streamer in the Stern of a Ship.

ancon.c: ANCON, is the Top or Point of the Elbow, and is taken also sometimes for the backward and larger (hooting forth of the V/na.

anconus.c: ANCONÆUS, a Muscle of the Cubit called ib by Riolanus, from its Situation. It ariseth fleshy from the Inferior and back part of the Os Ilumeri, growing larger as it marcheth between the superior ends of the Ulna and Radius, and is inserted fleshy to the lateral part ot the Brachi.cus External, a Thumb’s length below the Olecranum : It helps to extend the Cubit.

ancyloblepharum.c: ANCYI.GBLEPHARUM, is the growing of the Eyc-lids to the Tunica Cornea , or to the Albugitiea, so that sometimes both the Eye-lids grow together.

ancyloglossum.c: ANCYI OGLOSSUM.is when the little String under the Tongue is too straitly tied, so that there is a difficulty of uttering the words.

ancyrqides.c: ANCYRQIDES, the shooting forth of the Shoulder-Bones in the form of a Beak ; which is Called Coracoidcs, Anchoralis and Cornicularis,

andratomy.c: ANDRATOMY, is a Diilcetion of Humane Bodies, as Zootomy is of those of Beasts.

andromeda.c: ANDROMEDA , a Northern Constellation consisting of 27 Stars.

androgyne.c: ANDROGYNE, an Hermophradite, which is of both Sexes, or both Male and Female.- The same with

androgynus.c: ANDROGYNUS, an Hermaphrodite, or one who is Castrate or Effeminate.

anglicism.c: ANGLICISM, is the English Idiom, or form of Expression, or manner of Speech, which is peculiar to England.

anemoscope.c: ANEMOSCOPE, a Machine invented to foreshew the Change of the Air or Wind: 1 have observed that Hvgrolcopcs made of Cats-gut A N G (according to the Directions which sou will imd under that word) are very nice Anemoscopes and never fail hardly by their turning the Index about to foretell the Husting of the Wind. But as Vitruvius describes an Anemoscope , it shews that the Ancients rather designed it to Ihew which way the Wind blew, than to foretell to what Quarter it would shift or change. AN-JOUR & WAST, is a Forfeiture when a Man has committed petit Treason or Felony, and has Lands held of some Common Person, which lhali be seized for the King, and remain in his Hands a Year and a Day next aster the Attaindure; and then the Trees shall be pulled up, the Houses razed and pulled down, and the Pasturage and Meadows plowed up ; unless hetof whom the Lands should come by Escheat or Forfeiture redeem it of the King.

aneurism.c: ANEURISM, is a Disease which is a kind of Dilatation or bursting of the Arteries, always beating, and swelling sometimes to the bigness of an Egg, which yields, if you compress ir, bur recoils presently. The most Accurate and Learned Dr. Tyson sound in his Anatomy of the Tajacu or Aper Aiexicanus, several Ancurifmata in the Aorta or great Artery, which it seems were natural, and which he never saw before in the Arteries of any other Animal: Though Malpighim, as he observes, took notice of such in the Aorra of Silkworms.

angaria.c: ANGARIA, a Term in Law, signifying any troublesome or vexatious Duty or Service, paid by the Tenant to the Lord.

angild.c: ANGILD, the bare single Valuation or Compensation of a Man or Thing, according to the legal estimate, from the Saxon , An one, and gild Payment, Mulct, or Fine; so Twigild was the double Fine, Trigild the treble Fine, according to the rated Ability of the Person.

angiglossus.c: ANGIGLOSSUS, one that stuttereth or hath a Difficulty in his Speech of pronouncing L, R or R.

angina.c: ANGINA, a Quinsy or Squinancy, is an Inflammation of the Jaws or Throat, attended with a continual Fever and difficulty of Respiration and Swallowing, and it is two-fold ; either Spuritt or Exquisita, a Bastard or a true Squinsie : The latter is again four-fold, Synancke, Parafynanche, Cbynanche and Parachynanche .- Of all which in their proper places. Blanchard.

angle.c:
ANGLE, in Geometry, is either Plane or Solid. A Plane Angle is the Inclination, Aperture, or Distance between two Lines meeting in a Point. And which when the Lines forming it (which are

A N G A N G called its Leggs) arc Right or Strait ones, is called a Right lined or Rccii-lincnl Angle as B ; but when the Legs are crooked Lines, ’tis called a Curvi-lineal Angle as A and when one Legg is strait and the other crooked, ’tis called a Mixt Angle, as C. An Angle is usually marked with 3 Letters (especially if there be more Angles than one at the same Point,) whereof the middle Letter, which is always placed at the Angular Point where the Lines meet, denotes the Angle. The. Quantity , i.e. the Greatness or Smallness of an Angle is by no means measured by the length of its Legs, but by their Distance from or Inclination to each other. Thus the Angle L is le Is than A, though the Legs ol B are much longer than those of A ; but then thole of Bare more inclined to each other, than the Legs of the Angle A. Which to conceive the better, imagine the Angle A to be laid upon B, as the pricked Lines about B do represent ; then 'tis plain the Angle 3 will easily be contained within A ; and therefore is, less than A, because its Legs come nearer, or arc more inclined towards each other, than those of A : And consequently A will be a greater Ange than B, because its Legs are farther distant from each other than the Legs of B. If you imagine the Legs to open and shut like those of a joint-Rule, or a Pair of Compasses the thing will be very plain. The Quantity of any Angle is measured by the Number of Degrees of the Ark of a Circle intercepted between the Legs of the Angle, whose Center is the Angular Point. Thus Ark is the Measure of the Angle ach ; and 1 contain 30 Degrees, the Angle is said t Angle of 30 Degrees. f „ r nr rs A RECTI-LiNEAL ANGLE, is - «. Bight, when one Leg of the Angle stands exactly upright, or perpendicularly on ’ as fc doth on eh ; and inclines no more on «|T than it doth another. And such a ^ . j said to be an Angle of 9 ° Gegrees. because ^ ^ measured by an Ark that is the 4 * P Circle (as >ou lee in the last Figure) a Y Circle being supposed to have its whole Urcum science divided into 360 pares (which are called Degrees ) the 4th part of that, is 90 Dcgr. and therefore a Right Angle contains 90 Degr. 1. An Obtuse Angle , as aco, which exceeds or is bigger than a Right one, and is called Obtuse because its Angular Point is blunt. 3. An Acute Angle, as ach, which is less than a Right one, and is called Acute because its Angular Point is sharp. ANNALS', are a Chronological Account of the Remarkable Events of a State, yearly, as the Annals of Tacitus: They differ from History , because this descants upon those Events and on the Causes that produced them. annuapensione.c: ANNUA PENSIONE, is a Writ whereby the King having due unto him an Annual Pension from an Abbot or Prior for any of his Chaplains (whom he should think for to nominate, being as yet unprovided of sufficient Living) did demand the same of the Abbot or Prior ; and also willed him for his Chaplains better assurance, to give him his Letters Patent for the same.

annualequation.c: ANNUAL EQUATION, or mean Motion of xhc Luminaries. See Equation.

annualia.c: ANNUALIA, formerly a Yearly Stipend assign’d to a Priest, tor keeping the anniversary, or otherwise for laying continued Masses one Year, for the Soul of the deceased Person.

antaphroditickmedicines.c: ANTAPHRODITICK MEDICINES, are such as are used for the French-Pox.

antartickpole.c: ANTARTICK POLE, is the Southern Pole , or end of the Earth’s Axis ; ’tis so called because opposite to the Arctics or North-Polc.

antartickcircles.c: ANTARTICK CIRCLES: See Polar Circles. ANTARTHR 1 TICK MEDICINES, are such as are used against the Gout.

antasthmatickmedicines.c: ANTASTHMATICK MEDICINES,are such as are used against the Asthma, ANTECEDENCE IN. or in Antecedents : The Astronomers say, a Planet is in Antecedence when it appears to move, contrary to the usual Course or Order of the Signs of the i^odiaefi, as when it moves from Taurus towards Aries, &c. but if it go from Aries to Taurus and thence to Gemini, &c. they say it goes in Consequentia or in Consequence.

antecedent.c: ANTECEDENT (inLogickj) is the first of the two Propositions in an Enthymema , as the latter is called the Consequent.
ANTECEDENT, in Mathematicks, is the former of two Terms of Proportion , or that which is compared with the other; thus, if the Proportion were of A to B, A is said to be the Antecedent.

antes.c: ANTES, in Architecture , are Square Pilasters which the Ancients used to place at the Corners of the Walls of their Temples.

antestature.c:
ANTESTATURE, is a small Retrenchment made of Pallisadoes, or Sacks of Earth set up in G haste

anthelix.c: ANTHELIX, is the Protuberance of the Ear, or the inward Brink of the outward Ear, being a Semicircle within the Helix , and almost parallel to it,

anthelminticks.c: ANTHELMINTICKS, are such Medicines as destroy Worms.

anther.c: ANTHERÆ, are those little Tops or Knobbs which grow on the tops of the Stamina of Flowers, and are oftncr called Apices: Which see. Air. Hay Englilhes them Chives.

anthology.c: ANTHOLOGY, is a Discourse or a Treatise of Flowers, or the Art of a true Florist. ArYTHRACOSIS OCUL 1 , isa corrosive sea ly Ulcer in the Eye, attended with a general Tumour, especially of the Parts about the Eye.

anthrax.c: ANTHRAX, Car ho , Puma, or Carhuncuius, is defined to be a Tumour that arises in several places, surrounded with hot, fiery and most sharp Pimples, accompanied with acute Pains, but without ever being separated ; and when it spreads it self farther, it burns the flesh, throws off lobes of it when it is rotten, and leaves an Ulcer behind it, as if it had been burnt in with an Iron. Blancbard. ANT 1 AS, in the Plural Antiadcs, are the Glands called the Tonfills or the Almonds of the Jars. ANTIAPHROD 1 TICKS, are Medicines that lay Lust.

antiarthriticks.c: ANTI ARTHR 1 TICKS, are Medicines against the Gout.

antiasthmaticks.c: ANTIASTHMATICKS, Remedies against shortness of Breath, ANTl-BACHIUS, is a Latin Verse whose Foot con lists of three Syllables, the two first long and the last Ihorr.

anticardium.c: ANTICARDIUM, the same with Scrohicuius Cor dis. ANTiCTHONES, the same with Antipodes.

anticks.c: AN TICKS, in Architecture, are certain carved Works representing divers odd shapes of Men, Beasts, Birds, Fillies, Flowers, Ec. which being rudely determin’d and form’d one out of another, serve as an Ornament to that whole Fa brick, and afford a grateful variety to the Eye of the Beholder.

antidiluvian.c: ANTIDILUVIAN, is whatever was before Noah's Flood : Thus those Generations from Adam which were before the Flood are called the Antidiluvians , as those since descended from Noah are called the Post DUtivians. The Earth that then was before it was destroyed by the Flood, and which the Ingenious and Learned Dr. Tho. Barnes conceives to have been very different from ours in Form, Constitution, Figure, and Situation, is called .the Antidiiuvian Earth. But Dr. Woodward in his Natural History of the Earth , undertakes to prove from a Series of Observations, carefully made, 1. That the Face of the Earth before the Deluge was not as the Theorist imagines, Smooth, Even, and Uniform, but as it is now, Unequal, distinguished into Mountains, Valleys and Plains, as also having a Sea, Lakes and .Rivers. 2. That this Sea was Salt as ours is, agitated ly Tides, replenished with Pishes of all kinds, and that the Ocean then was nearly of the same Extent A N T and possessed an equal share of the Globe with the present one. That the Antidiiuvian Earth was stock d with Vegetables and Animals on all sides and int all parts of it quite round the Globe; had both Metals and Minerals in it; had the lame Position in respect of the Sun which ours now hath, its Axis being not parallel, but inclin’d as at present, to the Plane of the Ecltpcick ; and conlea uently there were then the lame Succession of [eat and Cold, Wet and Dry, and the same Vicissitudes of Seasons, Spring, Summer, Autumn and HAnter, as there are now.

antihecticumpoterii.c: ANTI-HECTICUM POTERII, or Jupitm’ s Diaphoretic!^, is a Chymical Medicine made by the mixture of Tin , the martial Regulus of Antimony and fixed by Sait-Peter. See the Operation in Loners s Chymistry, last Edit. p. 117. ANTIHYPNOT 1 CKS, Medicines that drive away Sleep. ANTI-HYPOCHON DRIACIvS , are Medicines used against the Hypochondriacs Melancholy.

antilogarithm.c: ANTI-LOGARITHM . the Complement of the Logarithm of any Sine, Tangent, or Secant to 90 deg.

antilogy.c: ANTI-LOGY , is a Contradiction between any Words or Passages in any Author.

antimetrical.c: ANTI METRICAL, is whatever is contrary to the Nature and Order of Metre or Verse.

antimoniumdiaphoreticum.c: ANTIMONIUM DIAPHORETICUM, is made of one part of Antimony and 3 of Salt-Peter powdered and mixed together, and thrown Spoonful by Spoonful into a Red hoc Crucible, a Detonation will follow each Spoonful ; when all is put in, continue a great Fire about the Crucible for about two Hours; then throw the white Matter in an Earthen Vessel of fair Water, and leave it steeping warm for about 12 Hours, that all the Salt-Peter may be dissolved ; then pour off the Liquor gently, and wash several times the white Powder at the bottom ; which is the Calx of Antimony, or Antimonium Diaphorcticum. The Dose is from 6 or 8 Grains to 30. Lemcry faith, he could never find it would raise a Sweat.

antimoniummedicamentosum.c: ANTIMONIUM MEDICAMENTOSUM, is a Preparation consisting of 5 Ounces of Antimony, 1 Ounce of Salt of Tartar, and 4Ounces of Salt-Peter fluxed together into a Bcgulus, winch is afterwards powder’d and was lid.

antimoniumresuscitatum.c: ANTIMONIUM RESUSCITATUM, » made of equal parts of Antimony and Sal Armoniack, sublimed together three times; then the Sublimate is wash’d with distill’d Vinegar warm co get out the Salts. ANTINEPHRI 1 ICK, isa Medicine good a* gainst the Stone.

antinomasy.c: ANTINOMASY, is a Figure in Grammar, or rather Rhetorick , whereby an Appellative is used instead of a Proper Name ; as the Philosopher instead of Aristotle, 8cc. and whatever is thus delivered or spoken is laid to be to delivered or spoken Antonomajlically.

antipfristaltick.c: ANTIPF.RISTALTICK, is a Motion by which the Excrements of the Guts are carried upwards instead of downwards, which is the usual and natural Peristaltic^ Motion. See chat word.

antipharmacum.c: ANTIPHARMACUM, the same with Anti dote, is a Medicine that expellsPoison.

antiphrasis.c: ANT1PHRAS1S, a figurative Speech, having a contrary meaning to what it carries in appearance. . . „

antipilepticks.c: ANT1PILEPTICKS, are Medicines against the Falling sickness.

antipodes.c: ANTIPODES, are such Inhabitants of the Earth as live diametrically opposite to one another, that is, in Parallels of Latitude equally distant from the Equator, but one North the other South ; and under the same Meridian, though i8o°. or 3 u st half of that Meridian distant from one another.
