ANTlPsOSlS, a Figure in Grammar, where11 Ann a ^' S P uc ^ or mother. in is a Term in Geography, signify Si such Inhabitants of the Earth as live in two P aces opposite to one another,one on the-iWr/j the tj 1 „ 011 foe South side of the Æijuator ; so that ^ shadows at Noon fall dis serene ways, onedic ct!y opposite to the other. ANTISCORBUTIC^ are Medicines against ine Scurvy. wh AN , TlSTR O p HH, is a Figure in Grammar, j ^ re “y two Terms of things which are mutual- > dependant one upon another, or reciprocally rte d ; as if one should say, the Master of AVrrr ant ’ an d the Servant of the Master, r. !i Sp ASMODICKS, are Remedies against '-onvujsions. tet!\^1^^ p NAR, one of the Muscles that ex AVT Thurab - t(ti n *^HES1S, in Rhctorick, is a setting two that s i Wa ^ Opposition one against another, Folly of i Rxccp cncc of one, and the Evil and ANTrr odter may the better appear, lower e / R AGUS, a little Prominence at the Traour n l ^ le / h it 'helix, seated opposite to the whence ir the Lcvatores , which distend and open the Anus in order to discharge the Excrements ; and one called the Sphin'dcr, which shuts it and keeps it so. There is also a Cavity in the Brain called Anus, which ariies from the four Trunks of the Spinal Marrow ; and by some the Skin which goes over the Navel, in aged persons becoming wrinkled is called Anus.

aorta.c: AORTA, or great Artery, so called because it is the greatest Artery in the whole Body, from which all others (except the Pulmonary) are derived : It rises immediately out of the left Ventricle of the Heart, and at its rife hath three j Valves which have the same tile arid figure as the Scmilunarcs in the Arleria Pulmonaria. As soon as the Aorta Comes out of the Heart, it ascends a little upwards, and then turns downwards ro ' form the descending Trunk, because the Blood ' might offend the Brain, if it ran .with that impetuosity with which it's thrown out of the Heart ; and from the upper side of this turning, th eCervical and Axillary Vessels do arise : By this Artifice, as the Blood collides against the sides of the Aorta, its force is brqken, part of it is taken in ! by the Mouths of the ascending Branches, but its ’ greatest part is directed downwards. At the rise of the Coionariæ out of the Aorta, there is a Valve placed that permits the Blood to flow out of the great Artery into them, but hinders its reflux, when it hath pierced the Pericardium and bended a little Arch-ways backwards, it is divided into two Trunks, whereof the one is called Irunctis Ascendent, the other Dcscendens, The Aorta hath sour Tunickj, a Nervous, a Gianduleus, a Muscular, and a Membranous one, which is the Internal,

apagogicaldemonstrations.c: APAGOGICAL DEMONSTRATIONS, are such as do nor prove the thing directly, but shew the impossibility arid absurdity which arises from denying it; and therefore *tis usually called Jstedttbh'o ad imppjsibilc, vel ad Absurdum.

apathy.c: APATHY, is an utter want of Passion.

apepsie.c: APEPSIE, bad Digestion, or rawness of Stomach, when there is no good Concoction of the Aliments.

aperienspalpebramrectus.c: APERIENS PALPEBRAM RECTUS, is a Muscle so called from its streight progress and use. It arises sharp and fleshy from die profoundest part of the Orbit, near the place where the Optick Nerve is transinitted, passing directly over the Mufculits Attollcns , it becomes Tendinous as it marches over the Bulb of the Eye ; whence growing still broader and thinner, till it is inserted to the whole superiour part of the tinner Eye lid.

aperitivemedicines.c:
APERITIVE MEDICINES, or such as onm G r the

A P I A P O the obstructed passages in the small Vessels , Glands or Pores, and by that means promote a due Circulation of the contained Juices.

aperturafeudi.c: APERTURA FEUD 1 , a Term in the CivilLaw, signifying the less of a Feudal Tenure by default of Issue of him to whom the Feud was first granted or given.

apertureinsomewritersofgeometry.h: APERTURE in some Writers of Geometry
apertureinsomewritersofgeometry.c: APERTURE in some Writers of Geometry is the Inclination of one Right Line to another, which meet in a Point and form an Angle. And "tis so called, because the Angle is the opening of the Legs of the Angle, like those of a Joint Rule.

aperture.c: APERTURE, in Qpticks, is the Hole next to the Object Glass of a Telescope or Microscope through which the Light and Image of the Object comes into the Tube and thence is carried to the Eye. Mr. Au sout faith, he found that the Apertures of Telescopes ought to be nearly in a Sub duplicate Proportion of their Lengths. The visible Area of an Object, is not increased or diminished by the greater or lesser Aperture of \ the Object Glass; all that is effected thereby is the admittance of more or less Rays, and consequently the more bright or obscure appearance of the Object. When you look at Venus through a Telescope, )ou must ule a much Ids Apettwe than for the Moon, Jupiter or Saturn, because her Light is so vivid and glaring. APE I ALOUS Flowers or Plants, are by the Botanists accounted such as want the sine coloured Leaves of Flowers which they call Petala .- These Flowers are otherwise called Stamineous, and are justly reckoned Imperfect.

apex.c: APEX, is the top, point, uppermost or sharpest part of any thing.

aphresis.c: APHÆRESIS, in Grammar, is that Figure which takes away a Letter or a Syllable from the beginning of a Word. In Surgery, is that part which teaches to take away Superfluities. APHEL 1 UM, ot Aphelion, or Auge, in the Copernican Hypothesis, is that point ol the Earth's or any other Planet's Orbit, in which it is the farthest distant from the Sun that it ever can be ; and when 'tis at its nearest distance, it is said to be in its Perihelion. Mr. Newton proves the Aphelia of the Planets as well as the Nodes to be at rest. Prop. 14 Book. 3. In Philoj. Tranjad. N. 128. is a strict Geometrical Method for finding the Aphelia of the Planets, by Mr. Halley.

aphorism.c: APHORISM, is a general Rule, or eminent but short Observation experienced for a Truth in any Art, or relating to Practice.

aphth.c: APHTHÆ, are Wheals, Ulcers or Pimples about the Internal Parts of the Mouth ; as also about the Ventricle and Guts, which when they come to be ripe, fall off bv piece-meal, and are often accompanied with a Fever in those of riper Years. Infants are much subject to the Aphtha;, they begin in the Gums, and by degrees spread over the whole Palate and Mouth ; if they le,re the Epiglottis and the upper parts of the Throat, the Child seldom recovers. These are the Aphtha: of Celfus,

apices.c: APICES, of a Flower, are those little Knobs that grow on the Tops of the Stamina, in the middle of the Flower : They are commonly of a dark purplish Colour. By the Microscope they have been discovered to be, as it were, a sort of Capful.e Sctninales or Seed Vessels ; containing in them small Globular and often Oval Particles, of various Colours and exquisitely formed, as I have often with Admiration observed my sols: In the Plant called Geranium Robertianutn or Herb Robert, these Apices are of a deep Purple Colour, and the Pulviscular Matter within of a glorious Yellow; they are exquisitely Spherical, and afford a very pleasant prospect in the Glass. What the Use of these so finely elaborated Particles is, is not yet, that I know of, discovered Some have guessed it co be a kind of Malc-Sperm, which falling down into the Flower, they will have to help foccundate and ripen the Seed ; but this I take to be a meer Fancy.

apnoea.c: APNOEA, a Depravation and Diminution, or an entire Suppression of Breathing, at least to Sense, as it happens in Swoonings, Fits of the Mother, and strong Apoplexies. APOCHYL 1 SMA, is any Juice boiled and thickened w.ih Honey or Sugar into a kind of hard consistence. This is called also Rob. Robub, and Succago.

apocope.c: APOCOPE, a Figure in Grammar, wherein the last l etter of a Word or Syllable is cut off.

apocrousticks.c: APOCROUSTICKS, are (according to some Physicians; such Medicines as hinder the Influx of the Humours to any particular part ©f the Body ; and reject thole which are beginning to flow thither. APOD 1 C riCAL Agument or Syllogism, signifies a p ain Proof or Demonstration 01 a thing. APOD 1 CTICK, the same with Apodidical . APODIOX 1 S, a Figure in Rhetorick, where* in any Argument or Objection is with Indignation rejected as absurd.

apogeeorapogum.c: APOGEE or APOGÆUM, in Astronomy, is the farthest distancqgthat any Planet can be at from the Earth in itAvhole Revolution; as Perig.cum is its nearest distance. How to find both Ap»g.vum and Perigœum fee the Geometrical Met host of Caffint, with some Considerations upon it by Mr. Mercato> , in Philoj. ‘Trans N. 57.

apogeeoftheequant.c: APOGEE of the Equant, is the farthest distance of it from the Earth, or that Point where the Circumference of the Equant is Intersected by the Linea Apsidum in the remotest part of the Diameter , as the Perigee of the Equant is the opposite point of the nearest part of the Diameter. The Mean

apogeeoftheepicicle.c: APOGEE of the Epicicle, is a point where the Epicicle is cut above by a Right Line drawn from its Center to the Center of the Equant, or the Point of the Epicicle most remote from the Earth.

apologetical.c: APOLOGETICAL. is what is said or written by way of Excuse or Apology for any Action.

apologue.c: APOLOGUE, is an Instructive Fable, like thole of Æsop. APOMEfoMETRlE, is an Art teaching the Practiler how to measure things at a Distance, vi%. how far they are off from him.

aponeurosis.c: APONEUROSIS, is (with Anatomists) the spreading or extension of a Nerve or a Tendon out in Breadth, in the manner of a Membrane: Also the cutting off a Nerve or Tendon is so called.

apore.c:
APORE , in Mathematicks, is a Problem which though it be not impossible, yet is very difficult

A P O difficult to be resolved ; and hath not yet actuI ally been so : Thus the Quadrature of the Circle way be called an Afore, because there is yet ho Way or Path discovered to lead us into it.

apophlegmaticalmedicines.c: APOPHLEGMATICAL Medicines, are such as are endowed with the Faculty of drawing cold pituitous Humours from the Head, and discharging them by the Nole or Mouth.

apophyge.c: APOPHYGE, in Architecture, signifies that part of a Column, where it seems to fly out of its Base like the Process of a Bone in a Man’s Leg, and begins to shoot upward. But this Apophyge is really no more than the Rings or FerriJs heretofore fasten’d at the Extremities of wooden Pillars to keep them from splitting, and afterward imitated in Stone work.

apophysis.c: APOPHYSIS, is a Protuberance made by the Fibres of a Bone, produced above its Superficies, and is ordinarily upon the Extremity of the Bones.

apoplexy.c: APOPLEXY, Attonitus, Stupor, Sidcratio, and Marbus attonitus, is a profound Sleep, wherein the Patient being either, vehemently shaken, tossed, or pricked, yet perceives nothing, nor affords any sign of Action ; accompanied with a difficulty of Respiration for the most part, and sometimes with none ar all. Bianchard.

aporrhe.c: APORRHEÆ, are Vapours and Sulphureous Effluviums which exhale through the Pores of the Body.

aporrheas.c: APORRHEAS, a word used by Mr. Boyle for Effluviums ; of the same Sense with the former.

aposiopesis.c: APOSIOPESIS (a Figure in Rbetorick) is when on a sudden a person changes his Passion, cutting off his Discourse so that the Hearer cannot easily imagine what it is he intends: As it is very common upon occasion of threatening, to say, J/T— &c. But, &c.—

apostareleges.c: APOSTARE LEGES, and Apoftatare Leges, signifies wilfully to break or transgress the Laws.

apostatacapiendo.c: APOSTATA CAPIENDO, is a Writ directed to the Sheriff, for to take the Body of one, who having enter’d into, and professed some Order of Religion, leaves it and departs from his House, and wanders about the Country.

apostrophe.c: APOSTROPHE, isa Figure in Rhetorick, when the Speaker in an extraordinary Commo- **°n, turns himself on all Sides, and addresses himself to all Beings, whether sensible or insensible. ; whom he, for the present supposes to be squally capable of hearing his Complaint, and of returning an Answer to his Demands.
APOSTROPHE, also, is an Accent in Gramshewing there is a Vowel to be rejected, is exprelYd thus (*) and paced over the Head of the Letter. Vofflus writes it Apostrophe. J

As the Apothegms ot Plutarch, or those of the Ancients C ° A^rvi Lycoflhenes. n , »OTOME, in Mathematics, is an Irrational Remainder, < r Residual Root j when from a ytfonal Line, as suppose a, you cut off a part A \ .h 1S only commensurable in Power co the 0 e Line. Then ’tis exprest thus a-— / b, and A P P is called Apotome, because it signifies a Remaindi t left by cutting off b.

apotome.c: APOTOME, in Musics*, is the difference between the greater and lesser Semitone.

apozeme.c: APOZEME, is a Decoction of Roots, Woods; Barks, Herbs, Flowers, Fruits, Seeds, Iso. which is boiled down commonly to Twelve, Fifteen, or Twenty Ounces. It is either Purging, Loo fining, Altering, or Drying, Cephaliclg, Stomachics Diuretics, Splenetics, or HepaticIg, according as the Indications of the Disease direct. _ APPARENT CONJUNCTION: See Co,ijunblion Apparent.

apparentplaceofastar.c: APPARENT Place of a Star, is a Point determined by a Line drawn from the Eye, through the Center of the Star; whereas the True or Real Place is determined by a Line drawn from the Center of the Earth to the Star or Planer.

apparentplaceofanyobjceiinoptickj.h: APPARENT PLACE of any ObjcEi in Optickj
apparentplaceofanyobjceiinoptickj.c: APPARENT PLACE of any ObjcEi in Optickj, is that (different from the real one) in which it appears when seen through one or more Glasses, For when by Refraction through Glasses, that parcel of Ra)s which falls on the Pupil of the Eye from each Point of any near Object is made to flow as close together as that which comes from a distant one ; or when by the lame way the Rays coming from distant Objects are made to Diverge as much as if they flowed from nigh ones, then the Eye must necessarily fee the place of the Object changed j which Change is its apparent Place. If an Object be placed nearer ro a Convex Glass than is the Distance of its Focus, its Apparent Place; and may be determined, as Mr.Afclyneux in Dioptr, p. 116 . shews. But if the Object be in the Focus of the Glass, the Locus Apparcns of the Object cannot be determined ; only as Dr. Barrow faith, it will appear vastly remote. Nor can the Locus Apparens be determined if the Object be beyond the Focus of a Convex: Glass. But if an Object be more distant from a Convex Glass, then its Focus, and the Eye lie beyond the diftinll Base, the Apparent Place of the Object will be in the diftintl Base .

appealofmayhem.c: APPEAL of Mayhem, (in Law) is an accusing of one that hath maimed another : Bur that being no Felony the Appeal is but a kind of Action of 'Trespass, because there is nothing recovered but Damages.

appeal.c: APPEAL (in LawJ is a removing of a Cause from an Inferiour Judge to a Supcriour: Also a private Accusation of a Murihercr, by one who had Interest in the murthered party ; or of any Felon, by one of his Complices in the Fact.

appealofwrongimprisonment.c: APPEAL of wrong Imprisonment , a Term in Law, is by some used for an Action of wrong Imprisonment.

appellant.c: APPELLANT, is he that brings an Appeal.

appellative.c: APPELLATIVE, a Term in Grammar, sig. nifying a Name in opposition to Proper, and which belongs to a whole Species or Kind, a§ Man, Chymiit . &c. AP PEL LOR or Appellant, the same with Approver,

appendantandappurtenantinlaw.c:
APPENDANT and Appurtenant f in Law) are things that by time or prescription have belonged, appertained, and are joyned to another principal thing, by which they pass and go as accessary

A P P A P P , K r r* accessary to the same special thing, as Lands, Commons, toa manner; Courts, Ways, &c. to a House, Office, or such others.

appendiculavermiformis.c: APPENDICULA VERMIFORMIS, so some Anatomists call the Intestinum Cæcum or Blind Gut, from its figure and manner of situation, which in some Animals hangs pendulous like a Worm, and is not filled with Excrement, as it is in others.

appensa.c: APPENSA, the lame with Periapta , such things as are hung about the Necks of diseased persons to free them from some Distempers which they labour under; such as a dried Toad to stop Bleeding, Peony Roots for Convulsions, &c.

appertinances.c: APPERTINANCES, lignific in the CommonLaw, things both Corporeal, belonging to another thing, as the more principal; as Hamlets to a chief Mannor, Common of Pasture, Turpary, Piscary, and such like j and Incorporeal, as Liberties and Services of Tenants.

applicate.c: APPLICATE, in Geometry, is a Right Line, otherwise called the Ordinate or Semi-ordinate in a Conies Section See the word Ordinate , or any Treatise of Conies Sessions.

application.c: APPLICATION, is sometimes the Geometrical Term for Division, the Reason of which fee in Geometrical Division. But Application also signifies the fitting or applying one Quantity to another, whole Area's but not Figures are the same. T bus Euclid, Book 6. prop. 28. teaches how to a Bjght Line given, to apply a Parallelogram equal to a Rehlilineal Figure given.

applicateordinate.c: APPLICATE ORDINATE (a Term in Geometry.) See Ordinate. It signifies a Right-line applied at Right-angles to the Axis of any Comck Section, and terminated by the Curve.

apportum.c: APPORTUM, in Law, signifies Revenue,Gain or Profit, which a thing brings in to its Owner.

apposaleofsheriffs.c: APPOSALE of Sheriffs, is the charging them with Money received upon their account in the Exchequer.

apposition.c: APPOSITION, in Grammar, is the putting of two or more Substantives together in the lame Case.

apprendre.c: APPRENDRE, in Law, signifies a Fee or Profit to be taken or received.

apprehension.c: APPREHENSION, is the simple Contemplation of things that present themselves to the Mind, as when we consider the Sun, the Earth, a Tree, Rotundity, a Square, Cogitation, Entity, pronouncing nothing expressly concerning them ; and the Forms under which they are considered are called Ideas.

approaches.c: APPROACHES, in Fortification, are Works cast up on both sides ; so called because the Besiegers by that means may draw near a Fortress without fear of being discovered by the Enemy. Or Approaches are all sorts ol Advantages by the help of which an Advancement may be made toward a place besieged.

appropriarecommunam.c: APPROPRIARE COMMUNAM, to disconv mon, that is, to separate and enclose any parcel of Land that was before open Common.

And to their Successors, so that the House or Body is both Patron or Parson, and some one of the Members officiates as Vicar. 'Tis called Appropriation, because the Profits of the Living are appropriate to the use of the Patrons.

appropriareadhonorem.c: APPROPRIARE ad HONOREM, a Term in Law, signifying, to bring a Man not within the extent or liberty of such an Honour.

approvement.c: APPROVEMENT, is where a man hath Common within the Lord’s waste Ground, and the Lord encloses part of the Waste for himself, having nevertheless sufficient Common, with egress and regress for the Commoners. This Inclosing is called Approvement.

approver.c: APPROVER (in Law) is he who hath committed some Felony, which he confesses, and to save himself impeaches his Accomplice or Accomplices ; and he is so called because he must Rove that which he hath alledged in his Appeal.

approversofthekjng.c: APPROVERS of the Kjng, are those that have the letting of the King’s Demeans in small Manners for the King’s greater Advantage.

arcanumiovis.c: ARCANUM JOVIS, is an Amalgama made of equal parts of Tin and Mercury, powder’d and digested with good Spirit of Nitre; and from it the Spirit being drawn in a Retort, the dry Mass is powdered again, and then digested with Spirit ot Wine, till the Powder be insipid.

archorark.c: ARCH or ARK, in Geometry, is any part of the Circumference of a Circle.

archesforthecourtofthearches.c: ARCHES for the Court of the Arches) is the chief and most ancient Consistory belonging to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and it is so called from the Arches of the Church where the Court is kept, namely, Bow-Church in London.

archeus.c: ARCHEUS, with the Patacelfians, is the Principle of Life, Health and Vigour in any Animal Body.

ARCH1PFXAGUS, in Geography, is a part ' H of

ARCH 1 TECTONICK, is that which builds a thing up regularly according to the Nature and Properties of it. Thus that Plastick Nature, Power, Spirit, or whatever it be called, which hatches the Ova of Females into Living Creatures of the same Species, is by some called the ArchiteRonick. Spirit.

architecture.c: ARCHITECTURE, is the Art or Science of Building, and is usually divided into Civil and Military. Civil Architecture teaches how to make any kinds of Buildings, Palaces, Churches, or Private Houses Military Architecture instructs us in the belt way to fortify Cities, Camps, SeaPorts, or any other Places of Strength. The Ancients at several Times, and on several Occasions, established 5 Orders of ArchitcRure, that is, 5 sorts of Pillars, vis'. the Tuscan, the Dorics, the Ionics, the Corinthian, and the Composite or Bptnan Order, ( Which fee under those Hords.) Tie Difference between which Orders, consists in the Column, with its Base and Capital and the Entablature, that is, the Architrave, Erise and Cornice ; for these are the Parts which constitute the Order, and each one hath its proper and peculiar Measures. Besides these 5 Ancient Orders, some Authors mention two more, as that of the Caryatides and the Persic^. (Which see.) The Rules of ArchitcRure require, that in a well-built Fabrick there should be Solidity, Convenience, and Beauty j to which some Writers add, Order, Disposition , Proportion, Decorum , and Oeconomy : And these Eight they make the necessary Parts of Architecture. Solidity, implies the choice of a good Foundation and good found Materials to work with. Convenience consists in so ordering and disposing the Parts ot an Edifice, that they may not hinder or embarrass one another. Beauty is that agreeable Form and pleasing appearance which it exhibits to the Eye of the Spectator, Order (they say) gives each part of the Building a convenient Bigness, whether we consider them apart, or with Relation to the Whole. And Disposition they make the due Ranging and agreeable Union of all the Parts. Proportion is the Relation that all the Work hath to its Parts; and which every one separately hath to the Idea of the whole: For amongst Works that are perfect, from any particular part, we may make a certain Judgment of the greatness of the whole Work: v. gr. the Diameter of a Pillar, or the length of a Triglyph, gives us a right Idea of the whole to which they belong. And to express the Relation that many things have to one another, as to their Greatness,- and the different number of their Parts, Vitruvius indifferently uses those three Words ; Proportion, Eurythmy, and Symmetry ; the two last of which are of much the lame Sense with the first. Decorum or Decency comes next to be considered, which consists in making the whole Aspect of the Fabrick so corrcR, that nothing shall apcar but what is founded upon, and approved of y some Authority and they say , Decorum teaches you to have a Regard to these 3 things; Design, Custom, and Nature. The Regard to De-. sign makes us choose (for Instance) other Dispositions and Proportions for a Palace, than a Church, The Respect we pay to Custom, makes us adorn the Porches and Entries into such Houses as arc within Rich and Magnificent. And the Regard we have to the Nature of the Places, makes us pitch upon different Prospects for different parts of a Building; as for example, we expose Bed-chambers and Libraries to the Morning Sun winter Apartments to the West, and Closets of Pictures, (sic. to the North, because they require an equal Light. Oeconomy teaches the Architect (they say) to have regard to the expenses that are to be made, and the Quality of the Materials, near the Places where he builds, and co take his Measures rightly for the Order and Disposition; vi%. to give the Fabrick a convenient Form and Magnitude.

The Summ of the Sides is 6x8=48. whose half is 24. which multiplied by 10 produces 240 Yards, the Area of the Hexagon. 7. For all Circles, multiply half the Circumference by the Radius ; because every Circle is equal to a Rectangle A, one of whole Legs is the Periphery , and the other the Radius. armed.c: ARMED, is said at Sea of a Man of War fitted out and provided in all respects. Also a Cross-Barr-Shott is said to be Armed, when sonic Rope-Yarn, or the like, is rowled round about one end of the Iron-Barr which runneth through the Short, both that the Short may be the better rammed down into the Gun ; and also chiefly, least the sharp end of the Barr should catch into any Honey Combs within the Cylinder of the Piece. A Load-stone is also laid to be Armed when it is capped, or cased, or let in Iron ; in order to make it take up the greater weight, and also to distinguish readily its Poles. Kjrcher in his Book de Magnete, tells us, that the best way to arm 2 Load-stone, is, to drill a Hole through the Stone from Pole to Pole, and in that to place a Steel Rod of a moderate length; which Steel Rod will, he faith, at the End, take up more Weigh 1 than the lame Stone armed the common way can do ; as he saw tried at Rome.

artery.c:
ARTERY : There are three kinds of Ducts in an Animal Body which bear the Name of A<- tery. The Asperia Artcria or Trachea, the Artcria Pulmonaris or Vena Arttrioja : Both which see. And most properly the Aorta, or great Artery, which carries the Spirituous Blood from the left Ventricle of the Heart, by its Branches, to all Pares of the Body. This, and its Ramifications are the only true Arteries. The word Artery, some say, is derived from dim n age ir, because ’cis concinuallyrising or moving with a Pulse like! Morion ; and may be defined co be an Organical and Similar Part, oblong and round, appointees to convey Spirituous Blood ro all Parts of the Body. The greatest Artery in the whole Body is the Aorta, for that reason often called the Artcria magna, and from it all the Arteries in the whole Body are derived, except th cArteria Pulmonaris . A brief Account of which, and how they spring from the Aorta I shall here subjoin. Before it comes out of the Pericardium it lends out sometimes one, but foin er two small Arteries, on each side one, which compass the Basis of the Heart like a Garland, in their Circuit, sending down divers Twigs lengthways on the Heart ; and these are called the Arteri<e Coronaria. When these two small Arteries have encompassed tha Basis and meet, they Inosculate one with another, but not with the Veins : Ac their rife out of the Aorta there is a Valve to hinder the Reflux of the Blood into the Aorta. These Coronary Arteries Dr. Ruyfch observes, send Branches ro the Auricles, and to the very Substance of the Heart it self j and to the Root of the Trunk ol the Aorta. The ascending Trunk then running up under the Vena Cam, lies upon the Wind-pipe, and presently fence ch forth two large Branches, whereof one passeth to the Right, the other to the Left Arm: They are called Rami jubdavii, because? they march under the Calvicule ; and as soon as they arc gone out of the Breast, are called Axili lares. The Right is the larger, and rising higher goes

ART A R 1 goes a more direct way towards the Right Arm ; the Left is less, and rising lower ascends more obliquely towards the Left Arm. They send out teveral Branches both from their lower and upper side. From the Lower proceeds the Superiour Intercostal, which runs along the Interstices or Intervals of the four uppermost Ribs, and fends Slips to the neighbouring Muscles and spinal Marrow. These sometimes are propagated from the Cerj vical Arteries, coming out through the Holes of the Vertebra'. From the upper side of each Sub c I avian springs first the Mamm.iria, which descends towards the Breasts through the Muscles that fill up the Interstices of the Cartilages of the true Ribs - and a considerable Branch of each descending out of the Thorax by the sides of the Caitilago enstfortnss, run down the Abdomen under the Mujculi Belli, spreading there into many Twigs, which are said to inosculate with the Extremities of the like Twigs of the Epigastrick Artery ascending. But that Opinion is io opposite to the Circulation of the Blood, that it is impossible to be true; for no Blood can ascend by the Mammari.e, nor descend by these ascending Twigs of the Epigastric. The next is Ccrvicalis (otherwise called Vertebral is) which lendeth Slips to the Vertebra and Muscles of the Neck, at whose seventh Vertebra it enters in by the Holes of the transverse Processes , and pierceth the Membrane that invests the Spinal Marrow, bestowing Twigs both on the Membrane and Marrow, and runs up therewith in at the great Hole of the Occiput, and being enter’d the Skull, both Branches (the Right and Lefts joyn under the Medulla Oblongata, and then are divided into innumerable, most small Twigs, which make wonderful NetLkc Plexus in the Pia Mater about the Cerebellum, and run into the Substance of the Cerebellum it self; and some of them being united with those of the Carotides make part ofthe very Bs te mirabile.- The third Artery that riseth out of the upper side of the Subclavian is Mujcula, which is spent on the Muscles of the Neck, and sometimes also on some of the Arm, After the Subclavians have had all these pairs of Arteries going out of them, they pass out of the Tvorax, and begin to be called Axillar, At the same place, or very near, where the ascending Trunk ot the Aorta sends out the Subclavians sideways, the remainder of it is divided into. two, called Carotides, which ascend directly upwards, (though the Right sometimes arise from the right Subclavian.) These ac their rise are sustained by the Ti.ymus, and having bestowed Twigs on the Larynx, Tongue, the Muscles of the Os Hjoidesj and the neighbouring Glands, pass up on each side by the sides of the Wind-pipe to the jayvs with the Internal Jugular Vein, and there arc each subdivided into the External and Internal Branches. The External is smaller, and is dispersed into all the Muscles of the Cheeks, Fore-head, Temples, Lips; and in general, through all the outer parts of the Head and Face. The Internal, which is larger, fends forth some more Twigs to the Larynx, Tongue, 8cc, as also to the Glands behind the Ears, and th& spongy parrs of the Palate and Nole. Then it entreth the upper Jaw, and bestows a (mall Slip on the Root of each Tooth (as the External did on the Roots of the Teeth ot the lower Jaw) whereby sharp Humours flowing in upon them sometimes cattle a very painful Tooth-ach. The remainder of it climbs upon the Skull, being about its Basts divided into two Branches: The lejs and hin- | der whereof having lent one Slip to the inner Muscles of the Neck, and another through the Hole of the uppermost Vertebra into the Membrane that invests the Spinal Marrow, ascending farther, enters the Skull, at the Hole by which the sixth Pair of Nerves (commonly so called J comes out, and creeping along the Dura Mater ends near its Sinus, (which yet some lay it enters.) The larger Branch, tending upwards, is carried through the bony Channel in the Wedgelike Bone with a winding Duct to the Sella equi - na ; at whose Basis, after it has lent out a Twig on each side into the Dura Mater, it opens it self into many small Slips, which being interwoven with those of the Cervical Artery (abovementioned ) make the Bete mirabile , which is more observable in Beasts than in Men. Yet it is nor all spent on the laid Slips, but perforating the Dura Mater, it enters the Pia Mater with two notable Branches, which being divided into very small Twigs, arc mingled with those of the Cervical Artery, with which they pass out ofthe Skull and accompany the Spinal Marrow even to the Loins.- Afterwards it fends a small Branch through the second Hole of the Wedge-like Bone with the Optick Nerve, out of the Skull to the Eye ; and yet still supplying more Twigs to the Substance of the Brain and Pia Mater, and being united with some other Twigs of the Cervical Artery, it makes the Plexus Choroides. The descending Trunk of the Aorta, which is larger than the ascending, goes down by the Gullet, to which it cleaveth. And hence is a Man that is hot, so much cooled with a Draught of cool Drink ; for the Gullet being cooled thereby, the Blood in the Aorta contiguous to it must needs be cooled likewise. ' Before it arrive ac the Diaphragm it sends out of its hinder side the inferiour lntcrcollals, which run along the Interstices of Eight or Nine of the lower Ribs, namely, those which the Superiour Intercostals did not supply. They likewise send Sprigs by the Holes of the Vertebra, made tor the Nerves, to the Marrow of the Back, and to the Muscles which rest upon the Vertebra, and also to those of the Thorax. Sometimes above this, and sometimes below it, there ariseth also out of the hinder part of the Aorta an Artery called Bronchialis, first found out and ib named by FrederickRuyfch, which accompanies all the Bronchia of the Wind-pipe. When it comes to the Midriff, there springs our of it the Phrenicx, one on each side; these running all through the Diaphragm, pass up into the Mediastinum , and sometimes into tlie Pericardium. Then having penetrated the Midriff it descends in one Trunk to the fifth Vertebra of the Loins» in which Pailage it first fendeth forth the Cœliaca, which arileth single, and is so called, because ^ fendeth Twigs to the Stomach. This springeth from the forepart of the Trunk at the hrst tebr*

ART ART tcbra of the Loins, and descending under the hollow of the Liver, upon the 1 runic of the Vena Porta, it is divided into two Branches, the and Left. The fight which is the smaller, ascending, produces in us upper part the Gaftrica dextra , that comes to the Pylorus , whence Sptgelius calls it P)~ Erica : And besides, the Cystic.e gcmclLc, which are very small, and are dispersed through the Gall Bladder. Hepaticx, which are two small ones: These are spent on the investing Membrane of the Liver (for its Parenchyma is nourished by the Porta) the Capfula Ccmmuuis, the Gall-Bladder and Po1 nts B ilarius. The remainder of this right Branch enters the Mesentery with many Twigs. The left Branch of the Caliaca, which is called Splenicus (sometimes springing immediately from the Aorta) is larger than the Eight, and as it goes towards the Spleen it lbndeth tonh ot its Upper side Gastrica mayor, which after it hath lusts-wed a Slip upon the upper and middle part ot the Stomach, is divided into two others; the hrlt whereof is called Coronaria Stomachica , which encompasses the upper Orifice of the Stomach like a Garland, and lends many Twigs to the Body ot the Ventricle it felt ; the other Gastric a finish a which '"according to Dicmcrbrocck, ) is carried cowards the Right-hand into the upper part ot the Stomach, and to the Pylorus. Out ot its °rver side spring, first Epiplois poitica, which runs to the hinder Leaf of the Omcntum, and the Colon annexed to it ; secondly, Epiplois sinifira, which is bestowed on the lower and lett side or the OTncntum . Just as this SplenicTc Branch is emring into the j Spleen, there ariseth out of its upper part Vas breve arteriojum, which goeth streight to the Jetc part of the bottom of the Stomach ; and the Gaftro*epiploisfinistra , Which being sustained by the upper or fore-leaf of the Omcntum^ sends ionic Twigs thereto, and s.lfo to the lett part of the bottom of the Stomach, and to both its fore and binder sides, then it enters into the Spleen. All these Arteries spring from the C At ac a, and accompany the Veins of the Porta of the like denomination. The next that arise tin out of the Trunk of the ^orta is the upper Mesenteries which springs from the fore-part of it as tjhe Cceliack, did. It accompanies the Vena Mcsai aica of the Porta, and runs through all the upper part of the Melentcry, and bestows many Branches on the Guts, Jejunum , Jleum , and that pate of Colon that lieth in the rj ght Hypochonder. Immediately below this, about the (second Vertebra of the Loins there go out of each side ot the descending Trunk of the Aorta an Ernulgent Artery, each of which being after its rife divided into two, and sometimes into three Branches, inters the Kidney on its own side. The Right springs out of it a little lower than the Left: both are subdivided into innumerable Twigs in the Parenchyma of the Kidneys, (all of which are invested with the Veins in one common Capfula borrowed from the Pelvis) and their Capillaries end in the Glands, wherein the Serum that these Arteries bring with the Blood is separated therefrom, and carried from them by the Urinary Siphons into the Pelvis. Next to these arise the Spermaticx (called Arterial prxparantcs.) These go out of the forepart of the Trunk very near together (very seldom either of them out of the Emulgents, as the left Spermatick Vein does) and the right passes over the Trunk of the Vena Cava: About two Fingers breadth from their rile they are each joined with the Vena prxparans of their own side, and descend with them, in Men, through the Process of the Peritonxum to the Stones, being divided into two Branches a little before they arrive at them, one of which runs towards the Epididymis, and the other to the Pest es. In Women , when they come near the Testes, (or Ovaria ) they are divided also into two Branches, one whereof goes to the Tcftcs, and the other to the bottom of the Womb. Next below the .Spermatick springs the lower Mesenteries om of the Trunk a little before it is divided into the semi Iliaci. This entreth the lower Region of the Mesentery, and distributes many Branches to the left paries the Colon, and to the streight Gut ; and lastly, descending to the Anus makes the internal Hemorrhoidal Artery. Very near to this, out of the Trunk still arise the lumbares, reckoned four in number; These go out of the backside of the Aorta, and are distributed not only to the neighbouring Muscles of the Loins, and to the Peritoneum, hut enters in at the Holes of the Vertebra of the Loins, and run along the Membrane that involves the Spinal Marrow, and penetrate into the Marrow it self. Besides these some reckon other two, on each side one, called Mufculx Superiores, (which run to the Muscles of the Abdomen ) unless these be two of the four called Lumbares. When the Trunk is descended as low as the fifth or last Vertebra of the Loins, and the top of Os sacrum, it begins to climb upon the Vena Cava, under or behind which it passed thus far : But as it begins to get upon it, it is divided into two equal Branches called fa mi Iliaci, and at its very division there springs out of it Arteria Sacra, whose small Twigs entring in at^he Holes of the Os Sacrum penetrate into the Marrow contained in it. The Trunk of the descending Aorta being divided into the semi Iliad , these arc subdivided presently into the interiour and exterieur Branches. From the interiour, which is less, proceed three others. First, The inferiour Muscula (called otherwise Glutxa) which is bestowed on the Muscles nam d Glutai that make the.buttocks, and also on the lower end of the Uiack Muscle and the Psoas. Secondly, The Hypogaftrick, , which is large, and at the lower end ot the Or Sacrum runs to the Bladder and its Neck, and the Muscles that cover the In Men it goes also along the two Nervous Bodies of the Penis as far as the

ART A S C the Glaus ; and in Women it is distributed in numerous Branches into the bottom of the Womb and its Neck, out of which, for the greatest part, issue the Menses in their monthly Purgation. It goes also to the Podcx, where it makes the external Hemorrhoidal Artery. Thirdly,TheVmbilicalArtery, which ascending by the sides of the Bladder, and being inserted into the Peritonaeum proceeds betwixt the two Membranes thereof to the' Navel, out of which it passes in a Fœtus in the Womb, and runs into the Placenta Vtcrina : But after the Infant is born, when there is no more use of it, it doles up, and turns into the nature of a Ligament, in some measure sustaining the sides of the Bladder, and hindring it from pressing on its Neck. prom the Exteriour Branch ot the Jsamus Iliacus two Arteries arise. First , The Epigastric 4 , which turning up wards on the outside of the Peritoneum runs betwixt it and the Mujculi Belli of the Abdomen as high as the Navel, where the Mammary Artery meets it, and according to Tradition ("though false) inosculates there with it. Secondly, Pudenda, which fends forth a notable Artery on each side into the Nervous Body of the Penis in Men, and into the Clitoris in Women. Hence it is carried inwards by the jointing of the Ossa Pubis to the Pudenda and Groins, and their Glands, and is spent en the Skin of thole parts, and of the Yard (in Men.) When all these pairs of Arteries have arisen out of the stami Iliad, they run down out of the Abdomen to (the Thighs, where they begin to be called C rurales.

arteriotomy.c: ARTERIOTOMY, is the artificial opening of an Artery for the letting of Blood in an inveterate Head ach, Madness, Falling-sickness, Pain and Inflammation in the Eyes and Ears, and the Section is made in the Fore head, Temples, or behind the Ears: The manner of it is thus; as ter the Ligature is made in the Arms or Neck, the Artery is cut just as a Vein is, and when the blood is emitted, you apply a very Astringent Plaister with a Leaden Plate to the Orifice, and then swathe it well. Blanchard.

arthritis.c: ARTHRITIS, Morbus Articularis , the Gout, is a Pain in the Joints of the Limbs, sometimes accompany’d with a miserable Contraction of the Nerves,Tendons, Ligaments,and thin Membranes about the Bones, with Swelling and Redness, and now and then with hard chalky Concretions. They account it four-fold : C hyragra the Hand Gout; Ifchias, the Gout in or about the Bone connected to the Os Ilium, which therefore some call the Hip-Gout: Gonagra, in the Knees; and Podagra, in the Feet.

arthritisvaga.c: ARTHRITIS VAGA, J Gout, which flies or moves from one Limb to another. ARTHRITlCK, or Arthritical , Gouty, diseased in the Joints, &c.

arthrodia.c: ARTFIRODIA , is the Articulation of one Bone into the shallow Sinus of another, as the Badius receives the Humerus,

artickpole.c: ARTICK POLE, is the North Pole of the World.

article.c: ARTICLE, in Arithmetics;, is ’sen, with all other whole Numbers that may be justly divided into ten Parts, as 20, 30, 40, £sc. they are sometimes called Decads, and sometimes Bound Numbers.
ARTICLE, in Grammar, is a small Word or Particle used to decline or vary the Gales, and to distinguish the Genders of Nouns and Pronouns, as Hic, Haec, Hoc in the Latin Tongue.

articulation.c: ARTICULATION, is that part of Grammar which treateth first of Sounds and Letters (which are called the Elements of Speech) and then of the manner of their Combination for the com po- « sing of Syllables and Words; so that he which pronounces his words clearly and distinctly, is laid to pronounce them Articulately. And such Sounds as can be expressed by Letters, and which form Words, are called Articulate Sounds.- ARTICULATION, in Anatomy, is a Conjunction of the Limbs of an Animal Body, for the due performance of Motion: Some make this two-fold, vst. Diarthrosts, which is a more loose, 1 and Synarthrojis, which is a more close Conjun - | hon. s The Term is also used by the Botanists for the Joints or Knots that are in some Siliqu.t, as those I of the Ornithopolium, and in the Roots of the f Polygonatum, and the Distance or Space between ; Knot and Knot, or Joint and Joint they call the | Interwdium. t

asperaarteria.c:
ASPERA Arteria , or Trachea , is an oblong Pipe consisting of various Cartilages and Membranes, which begins at the Throat, or lower part of the Jaws, lies upon the Gullet, descends into the Lungs, and is dispersed by manifold Ramifications , or Branches through their whole Sub! stance: The Upper part is called Larynx, and the Lower Bronchus, to which Malpighius adds a third, or lowest, called by him Vesicular : Ic is subservient to Speech and Respiration. That part of the Ajpcra Arteria which is called the Bronchus, contains all of it but the Larynx ; being the Body of the Pipe as well before as after its Insertion into the Lungs, all the Cartilages of this Bronchus are like the lowest of the Larynx, to which the uppermost of the Bronchus adheres, These Cartilages are seated one below another at equal distances, and keep in their places by both the Membranes of the Trachea , which sill up their Interstices, and tye them one to another like Ligaments. Yet these Rings have not their Circle Inure, but on the backside of the Bronchus next the Gullet, that they might give way to the Meat in swallowing, they pass into a Membrane, so that they are in figure like the Letter C. But this Interstice in their Circle, which most Anatomists affirm to be Membranous; Cafp. Bartholin (after his Father) says, is rather Carnous Fibres that run from one side or end of the Cartilage across to the other, which in Expiration (especially violent) contracting themselves, draw the ends of the Cartilage towards one another on each side, and thereby straiten the Pipe of iheTrachea. And though the Cartilages, so far as they are contiguous to the Gullet, (being about twenty in number) arc thus semi lunar as it were; yet those ol the Branches ot the Bronchus within the Lungs have no Interstice in their Circumference, being all Cartilaginous, though nor all of a Circular Figure, but some Four-square, other Triangular, Lse. as Diemerbroeck^ observes, the inner Membrane is plentifully beset with tniliary Glands, out of which good part of that mucous matter that bedaubs its inside issues, for the lubricating of it. The cmter Membrane helps to connect the Cartilages the more firmly one to another, and the whole Trachea to the neighbouring parts , that it may more safely and firmly descend into the Thorax. This is much thinner than the other; for the inner (according to Dr. PVillis) has two Rows of Muscular Fibres, the outer streight, the inner oblique, the first by their Contraction shorten the Trachea, the latter straiten it; so that he thinks they assist Expiration, especially when it is violent, as is coughing and hawking, or the like. Yet he says, this inner Membrane has two others growing upon it, as it were, one glandulous, and another vascular. Through this latter do the Bloodvessels and Nerves every where run ; and the Glands placed in the former receive and keep all the superfluous Moisture or Lympha deposited by the Arteries, which the Veins do not imbibe, till they can remand it by the Lympheducts (which spring from them) or if it be over plentiful, so that the Lympheducts cannot receive it all, then it issues both out of these Glands, and out of the Arteries into the Cavity of the Wind-pipe, and causes a Catarrh. But the inside of this Membrane is naturally moist, being besmear’d with a fattish and mucous Humour, to hinder its drying, and to make the Voice smoother; so that when this Humour is fretted off in Catarrhs, or the inside of this Membrane becomes rough from any i f easels

ASS ASS cause, the Voice becomes hoarse; and when it is dried by too much Hear, as in Fevers, it becomes squeaking. The Afpera Arteria has Veins from the external Jugulars. Arteries from the Carotidcs, and from the Arteria Bronchialis, (first found out by Frederics ctuyfch) which springs from the backside of the descending Trunk of the Aorta, a little above the lower Intercostals. Nerves it receives from the recurring Branches ot the par VagUm, which run mostly along its inner Membrane, whence it becomes so exquisitely sensible. When it is descended as low as the fourth Vertebra of the Thorax, it is divided into two Trunks, whereof one goes into the right Lobe of the Lungs, the other into the left, and each is presently again divided into two, and those into others, till at last they end in very small Branches, which are dispersed among the like Branches of the Pulmonary Artery and Vein, and end into and are continued with the little Bladders that make up the greatest part of the Bulk of the Lungs .

asperifoli.c: ASPERIFOLIÆ (Plant æ) is one of the Divisions or kinds of Plants: (Sets Plants, N. n.) In this kind of Plants, the Leaves stand alternately or without any certain order on the Stalks: The Flowers arc monopetalous , but having the Margin cut into 5 Divisions, sometimes deep, \ sometimes shallow; and the upper Spike or top of the Plant is often curved back something like a Scorpions Tail. They are called Afperifoliie because they are usually rough leaved, but they are not always so. After each Flower of this kind of Plants, there usually succeed four Seeds.- There being only the Cerinthe reckoned by Mr. Ray to belong to this Genus, which hath less than four Seeds at the Root of each Flower, but that hath but two. The Herba Afperifoliæ are, the Pulmonaria Mactdo/a , Cynoglojsa, Borago, Buglojsa, Anchuja, Echiwn, Linurn XJmbilicatum, Heliotropium majus, Aparine major, Confolida major, Lithojpermum, Echium Scorpoidcs and Cerinthe.

asperity.c: ASPERITY, is the inequality or roughness of the Surface of any Body, whereby some parts of it do so stick out above the rest, as to hinder one's Hand, (sic . from passing over it easily and freely.

asphyxia.c: ASPHYXIA, or a Cessation of the Pulse of the whole Body, is the highest degree of Swooning, and next to Death.

aspiration.c: ASPIRATION, is the pronouncing of any Syllable or Word strongly, with a good deal of Breath and some Vehemency; as we do those Words which have the Letter H before them, as have, hear, heat, &c. whereas they are sounded much softer and easier without the as ear , cat, &c..

aspyxia.c: ASPYXIA, a sensible decayed Pulse, the same with Asphyxia.

assart.c: ASSART, a Term in Law, signifying an Offence committed in the Forest by the plucking up the Woods by the Roots: Also to make Glades in a Wood, to grub up or clear a Ground of Bustles and Shrubs, (sic. or to lop off the Boughs of a Tree.

assation.c: ASSATION, is a Term in Pharmacy, used for a peculiar kind of Decoction or Boiling of their own Juice.

assaultintheartofwar.h: ASSAULT in the Art of War
assaultintheartofwar.c: ASSAULT fin the Art of War) is taken alto for a general Attack made upon a Fortress to get it by main force, without defending themselves in the Attack by any Works: The words are, to give an Assault to such a Place ; to be commanded to the Assault ; to fland an Assault, to Jecond an Assault ; to repulse an Asault ; to carry by Afault, &c. While an Assault lasts, and both Parties are mixt, there is no fear of Cannon on either side, for they are afraid of destroying their own Men thereby.

assetsinlaw.c: ASSETS fin Law) signifies Goods enough to discharge that Burden which lies upon the Executor or Heir, in satisfying the Testators or Ancestors Debts or Legacies,

assewiare.c: ASSEWIARE, signifies, to draw or drain out Water from a Marlliy Ground.

assign.c: ASSIGN (a Law Term) is he that is appointed or deputed by another to do any Act, or perform any Business, or enjoy any Commodity: And it is either in Deed or in Law.

assignindeed.c: ASSIGN in Deed, is he that is appointed by the Person himself.

assigninlaw.c: ASSIGN in Law, is he whom the Law so makes, without any appointment of the Person.

assimilation.c: ASSIMILATION, is a Term in Anatomy, by which they express the change that is made either of Chyle into Blood, or of the Nutritious Juice into the Substance of an Animal Body. Thus the Modern Anatomists say, Sanguification is not performed by the Liver only, as the Ancients supposed, but by a gradual changing of the Chyle into Blood by frequent Circulations, and the manner of this Change they call Assimilation,

assisacadere.c: ASSISA Cadere, in Law, signifies to be Nonsuited.

assisacontinuanda.c: ASSISA Continuanda, is a Writ directed to the Justices assigned to rake an Assize, for the continuance of a Cause, where certain Records alledged cannot in time be procured by the Party that would use it.

assisaproroganda.c: ASSISA Proroganda, is a Writ directed to the Justices of Assize, for the stay of Proceedings, by reason of the King’s Business, wherein the Party is employed.

atmosphereofconsistentbodies.c: ATMOSPHERE of Consistent Bodies .- The Honourable Mr. Boyle hath written a small Essay on this Subject, in which h-e proves, that very many, and therefore probably all solid, firm and consistent Bodies (i. e. such as arc not Fluid) have at some certain times fat least) effluvia of Particles of Matter which exhale from them : For he found, that many such Bodies would in a little time be very sensibly diminished in Weight: That some Eicllrical Bodies, as Amber and Glass, would exert that Property, uniformly all round them when they were heated; which they usually exhibit upon Rubbing or Chafing ; vi^. That of Attracting small Bodies to them: That Glass, Stones, and hard Metals would, on being rub’d one against another strongly emir, not only sensible, but even offensive Odours, &c.

atome.c: ATOME, is such a very small Particle of Matter, that it cannot Physically be cut or divided into seiser Parts: Epicurus and his Sect of Philosophers, first called the Component Principles of all Bodies, which they supposed to be infinitely small and hard, by this Name of Atoms. These Atoms may be supposed to have these 4 Inseparable Properties. 1. That they are all of the same Nature, Substance, or Matter ; for all Matter abstracted from Form is the same. 2. That they have all some Magnitude or Quantity ; for they are not Indivisible Points, but Physical Bodies of some (though small) determinate Bulk. 3. They have also all of them some determinate Figure or Shape. And 4. They must have also, each of them,, some real Gravity or Weight; To these Sextus Empiricui adds dejincrta. or fie nitency, but this rather may be supposed to be the Consequence of their being Solid and In/ctlile, which they are as they ar e Atoms. The Original Qualities of Atoms can only be their Si^e and their Figure, and these taken together make their Form,

attenuation.c: AT TENUATION, or lessening of the Power or Quantity of the Moi bisick Matter. Attick, a kind ot Order in Architecture, aster the manner of the City ot Athens. Vitruvim makes it the Name of a Basis, which the Modeni Architects have since given to the Dcrick Pillar. In our Buildings, the At tick. is a little Order placed upon another much greater, having, instead of Pillars; nothing but Pilasters of a particular form or fashion.

attire.c: ATTIRE, the Heralds call the Horns of d Stagg or Buck his Attiic.

ATTIRE, in Botany, signifies, according 16 Dr. Grew, the third part belonging to the Flower oi a Plant; of which the two former are the Empale-* rnent and the Foliation. This Attire' he finds to be of two kinds, Semini-form and Florid ; the Semiui - form Attire consists of two parts, Chives for the Stamina, as some call them) and Semcts or Apices, one upon each Attire. The Florid Attire is usually called Thrums , as in the Flowers of Marigolds Tanjey, &c.. These 'thrums the Dr. Calls Suits ^ which consist of two,but most times of three pieces; the outer part of the Suit is the Floret, whose Body is divided at the top like a Cowslip Flower into S Parts, or distinct Leaves. A 1 TGLLENS Auriculartt, is a Muscle which consists of divers fleshy Fibres, and is annexed to that part of the Pericranium that covers the Temporal Muscle, whence it descends directly to its Implantation at the Superiour Part of the second Wrinkle of the Cartilage of the Ear. Its Name shews its Use.

attollensoculos.c: ATTOLLENS Oculos, or Superbus, one of the six Pair of Muscles that belong 10 the Eye, serving to list them upwards. ATTOLLENS Narcs > a Muscle of the Nose, whole Name shews its Use.

attollentes.c: ATTOLLENTES, are a Pair of Muscles, which acting both together, draw all the upper Lip directly upward and outward; but if only one, then one side of the Lip is drawn obliquely. AT TO N 1 T U S, Stupor, feu Alorbus Attonitus : See Apoplexy.

attornatofacicndovelrecipiendo.c: ATTORNATO facicndo vel recipiendo, is a Writ which a Man owing Suit to a County, Hundred; Wapentake, or other Court, and desire ing to make an Attorney to appear for him, whom he doubtetb, whether the Sheriff or Bayliff will admit or : not, purchase th to command him to receive and j admit him. ATTOURJ3 MENT (in Law) is when one is Tenant for term of Life, and he in Reversion or Remainder grants his Right or Estate to another, then it behoves the Tenant for Life to agree thereto z and this Agreement is called an Attournment.

attracting.c: ATTRACTING; or Drawing Medicines or Things, are thole which opening the Pores with their little Particles, and dilating the Humours, and expelling them, where their Resistance is smaller, nor only slews the Parts; and makes them Red, but by driving more Vapours and Humours out of the Skin and Flesh, than can make their way through the thick inner Skin, gather them under it, and swell it into little Bladders.

attraction.c:
ATTRACTION, is the drawing of one thing to another. Whether among the Operations of Natural Bodies one upon another, there be any properly so speaking, is a Questions

ATT AUD a Question thac hath been much debated amongst Philosophers.- And perhaps moll of those Effects which the Ancients, not knowing so well the Causes of, did uric to attribute to Attraction may tow be very well solved by Passion. See James Beniotdi , de Gravitate Æthcris, Amsterdam 1683, in 8". However the word is retained by good Naturalists, and in particular, by the Excellent Mr. Isaac Newton in his Principia ; but without there determining any thing of the Quale of it, for he doth not consider things so much Physically as Mathematically. This therefore being promised, he lays it down as an Axiom ; That since Albion and Rc-action are always equal and directly contrary to each other ; therefore if any thing Attract another, it is its self also as much attracted by that other thing ; taking Attraction in the largest and most general Sense, for the Conatus of one Body towards another however it be caused. And in Cor. 1. Prop. 58. he shews, 1. That if two Bodies mutually do attract each other (by which he means the lame as gravitate towards one anorhei) by Forces proportionable to their Distances, they will describe both about the common Centie of Gravity, and about one another Concentrical Ellipses; and vice versa, if any Body do describe such Figures, their Gravitating or Attracting Forces are proportional to their Distances. 2. That if they Attract each other with Forces proportional to the Squares of their Distances, they will describe both about the Common Centre or Gravity and also about one another, Conicli Sections, having their Umbilici in the Centre about which the Figures are described ; and vice versa, &rc. 3. He demonstrates also, That any Particle of Matter within the Superficies of any Sphere or Globe is attracted or gravitates by a Force proportional to its distance from the Centre; but without the Surface of the Sphere, by a Force proporrionai to the Square of its Distance from the Centre. Prop. 73, 74. Lib. r. Hence it will follow, he faith, 1. That at equal Distances from the Centre of Homogencai Spheres, The Attraction will be as the Sphere. 2. And at any Distance whatever, the Attraction is as the Sphere divided by the Square of the Distance. 3. Which last holds also in the Attractions of Spheres towards one another; i. e. the Attractions arc as the Attracting Globes divided by the Squares of the Distances, though the Globes mutually attract each other. The Quantity of the Force of Attraction in all Bodies ac equal Distances is exactly proportionable to the Quantity of Matter in the Attracting Body, as being in reality nothing but the Result or Summ of the united Forces of all those single Particles of which it is composed.

attribute.c: ATTRIBUTE, is whatever Property belongs properly to any Substance or Being, and is affirmed of it, or duly attributed to it, or predicated of ir, as the Logicians speak.

attrition.c: ATTRITION, in Physick, is the Rubbing of one thing against another; as when Amber' and other E.ec trick Bodies are rub’d to make them attract, or emit their Electrick Force.

ATTRITION, in Theology, is a Sorrow for offending God, arising from the Apprehension of being obnoxious to Punishment and Misery on the Account of such Offence. AT I URN EY, or Attorney, in a Legal Acceptation, signifies, one appointed by another Man to do any thing in his stead, and is as much as Procurator or Syndicus in the Civil Law ■ or Atturneys are such Persons, as are by the Consent, Commandment, or Request ot another, to take heed, fee to, and take upon them, the Charge of another Alan’s Business in his absence. AVAN 1 Fosse, or Ditch of the Counterscarp, in Fortification, is a Moat or Ditch full of Water running round the Counterscarp on the outside next the Campaign, at the Foot of the Glacis. It is not eligible to have such a Waier-Ditch where it can be drained dry; because it is a Trench ready made for the Besiegers to defend themselves against the Sallies of the Besieged. Besides, it hinders putting Succours into the Place, or at least makes it more difficult so to do.

avast.c: AVAST, a Word used very commonly aboard a Ship, signifying to stop, hold, or stay.

audiencecourt.c: AUDIENCE Court , is a Court belonging to the Archbishop of Canterbury, of equal Authority with the Arches Court, though inferiour both in Dignity and Antiquity. AUD 1 ENDO 65 1 Tcrminando, is a Writ, but more properly a Commission, directed to certain Persons, when any Riotous Assembly, Insurrection, or heinous Misdemeanour, or Trespass is committed against any Place.

auditaquercla.c: AUDITA Quercla, is a Writ that lies where one is bound in a Statute, or Recognisance, or where Judgment is given against him for a Debt, and his Body in Execution thereupon ; then if he have a Release, or any other sufficient Discharge, but has no Day in Court to plead it, then he shall have this Writ against him which hath recovered, or against his Executors.

auditorynerve.c: AUDITORY Nerve , is the seventh Pair of Nerves that comes from the Medulla Oblongata , arising from the hinder part of the Proceffus AnnUlaris ; it enters the Hole in the inner Process of the Os P etrosum. It divides into two Branches; that which is soft is called Portio Mollis , and it is distributed into the Labyrinth, Cochlea, and Membranes which cover the Cavities of the Ear. That which is hard, is called Portio Dura ; it goes out of the Ear by the Hole which is between the Procejfus Mastoides and Styloides ; it is divided into two Branches, of which one goes to the Muscles of the Tongue, or Os Hyoidet, and it gives a small Branch to the eighth Pair ; the other is distributed in the External Ear, Nose, Lips, and Cheeks.

auditor.c: AUDITOR, according to our Law, is an Officer ot the King, or some other great Period which yearly, by examining the Accounts of all under Officers accountable, make up a General Book; with the Difference between their R e ' ceipts and Charge, and their Allowances, commonly called Allocations ; as namely, the Auditors of the Exchequer take the Accounts of those Receivers, who collect the Revenues of the AugtnenI ration, as also of the Sheriffs, Elcheators, Collectors, and Customers, and set them down, and perfect them.

auricui.c: AURICUI.Æ Cordis, are two Appendages to the Heart, seated at its Basis over the Ventricles; they arc so called from some Resemblance that they bear to the Ears of a Man’s Head. They arise from a long Basis and end in an obtuse Point, thereby forming an obtuse Triangle. They are of the same Fabrick and use with the Ventricles over which they stand, being Muscles as they are, made up of the faille order ot Fibres, which are carried into opposite Tendons; whereof that at the Basis of the Heart is common to it and the Auricula, and the other runs along their upper part. The Right Auricle is larger and loiter than the Left. The Superficies of both is smooth when they are full, but wrinkled when empty , and more so in the Left than in the Right one. On being cut open they exhibit many fleshy Columns running from the Upper Tendon to the Lower, and between them there are pretty deep Furrows or long Cavities, but fewer in the Right Auricle than in the Left. They are dilated and contracted in like manner as the Heart is, but at different times; for the Systole of the Ventricles is at the same time with the Diastole of the Auricles and vice verfri ; so that the Auricles are receiving their Blood from the Veins, while the Ventricles are expelling theirs into the Arteries : But when the Ventricles are relaxed and empty in their Diastole , then the Auricles force the Blood into them by their Systole, They are nourished by Branches of Arteries springing from the Coronaria, which Dr. Ruyfch (who seems first to have taken notice of this) calls therefore Arteries Auriculares ; and no doubt but they have Branches also of Veins to attend them. Their Use is to receive the Venal Blood which comes immediately out of the Vena Cava and Pulmonaris , and to measure it as it were (faith Gibson ) into the Ventricles: and to expel it thither with the greater force, the Internal Fibres or Columns of their Cavity arising from their Root where they arc joined to the Basis of the Heart, reach d irectly outwards towards the Vena Cava and Pulmonaris ; and in the Diastole of the Auricula: grasp the Blood contained in their Cavities like so many Fingers, and squeeze it into the Ventricles, now relaxed in their Diastole.

AURI PIGMENTUM, yellow Arsenide. AU RUM Fulminant , or Saffron of Gold , is thus made; Put a drachm of thin Plates of Gold into a Matrass, and then pour on it by little and little (or else there will be so great an Effervescence, that the Matter will boil over the Glass) 3 or 4 drachms of Aqua Regalis. Set the Matrass in warm Sand, and when the Ebullitions arc over, the Menstruum Will have dissolved as much of the Gold as it can contain. Pour off the Solution by Inclination into another Glass, and then Pour into it about 4 or s times aS much coisimon Water as there was of the Dissolution, and then drop into the Mixture, gradually, some of the Volatile Spirit of Sal Armoniach, or Oyl of Tartar per deli - quium, and the Gold will precipitate to the Bottom of the Glass: I.ct it stand a while till all is fallen down, then pour off the Liquor, an^Wash the Powder carefully with warm Water riff it grows insipid : Then dry it in a Paper by a gentle Fire, taking care it do not sire, which ’cis apt to do with K. 2 terr bis

A U T A X I terrible Noise. If you dissolve a drachm of Gold there will be 4 Scruples of Aurum Fulminans well dried. It takes its Name from its fulminating or making a great noise like Thunder, when ’tis heated over the Fire in a Spoon, for it will go off like a Gun, but without doing any Mischief, its Force being chiefly downward. The Effect seems to come from some parts of the Aqua stegalis, which remain still sticking in the Gold, and who being of a very Spirituous and Volatile Nature, do break out with great Violence, when the Powder comes to take Fire. Those who would know a way to make as great, but ;et a much less expensive Noise, may lee the word Pulvis Fulminans. If half its weight of Sulphur powdered be mingled with Aurum Fulminans, its fulminating Quality will be destroyed. Though on several Trials designedly made to make Gun-powder take Fire in Mr. Boyle's exhausted Receiver, it could not be effected ; yet he found that Autum Fulminans would take Fire there and go off', both by means of a Burning glass, and of a Piece of hot Iron.

aurummojaicum.c: AURUM Mojaicum , is made by mixing and subliming Mercury, Tin, Sulphur, and SalArmoniack all together. AUSTERE T ail, is such an one as moderately constringes the Mouth and Tongue with some Asperity, as is the last of unripe Fruits.

australsigns.c: AUSTRAL Signs, are the six last Signs of the ^odiaclt; so called, because they are on the South side of the Equinoctial.

authenticks.c: AUTHENTICKS: The word Authentici signifies, of good Authority ; and therefore the zd Volume or Tome of the Civil Law is called The Authentickj, from the Greek word avTiyfiy ; because it hath its Authority from it self, and proceeding from the Emperour’s own Mouth; or else that they are Originals to other Writings which are transcribed out of them. They are a Volume of new Constitutions, set out by Justinian the Emperour, after the Code, and brought into the Body of the Law under one Book. There is not in these that good Order and Method observed as there is in the Code or in the Digest ; but as any doubtful Point came to be considered, you have here the Princes Determination of it - and that let down as the Cases occasionally occurred. The whole Volume is divided into Nine Collations, Constitutions, or Seblions (I mean in the Latin Version, for in the Greek there is not this Division into Collations ;) and these are subdivided into 168 Novels, each of which is distributed into several Chapters. They are called Novels because they were New Larvs in comparison of the Code and Digest ; just as the Constitutions of the Emperours, which were newly published after the Basilica, were called the Novels of Leo , Nicephorus, Michael, 8cc.

autography.c: AUTOGRAPHY, is the peculiar Hand Writing of any particular Person ; or the Original of any Treatise or Discourse, in respect of a Copy.

automata.c: AUTOMATA, are Mechanical or Mathematical Instruments or Engines, that going by 4 Spring, Weight, f '§c. seem to move of themselves, as a Watch, a Clock, &c.

azimuthcompass.c: AZIMUTH Compass, is an Instrument made in a large Brass Box, with Jambols and a broad Limb, having 90 deg. diagonally divided, with an Index and Thread to take the Sun's Amplitude or Azimuth, in order to find the Difference between the Magnetical Meridian and the Sun's Meridian , which shews the Variation of the Compass.

azimuths.c: AZIMUTHS, or Vertical Circles, are great Circles intersecting each other in the Zenith and Nadir , (as Meridians or Hour-Circles do in the Pole) and cutting the Horizon at Right Angles. On the Globes these Circles are not drawn, but are represented by the Quadrant of Altitude when it is screwed in the Zenith. And on these Azimuths is reckoned the Sun’s Altitude, when he is not on the Meridian.

azoth.c: AZOTH, among the Chymists, signifies sometimes an Universal Medicine, sometimes the Mercury of a Metal.

azure.c: AZURE, the Heralds Term for a Blue Clolour in the Coats of all Persons under the Degree of a Baron ; but in the Escutcheons of the Nobility ’tis called Saphir3 and in those of Sovereign Princes ’tis called Jupiter. In Engraving ’tis represented by Strokes or Hatches drawn only Horizontally, thus.

azugosorazygos.c:
AZUGOS or AZYGOS, is a notable Branch of the Vena Cava, called also Vena fine pari, because it is single, having no Fellow. It descends through the right side of the Cavity of the Thorax, and when ’tis come as far as the Eighth or Ninth Vertebra , it begins just to keep the middle, and fends forth on each side Intercostal Branches to the Interstices of the Eight lowest Ribs, and there is divided into two Branches, of which the Larger descends to the Left, betwixt the Processes of the Diaphragm, and is inserted sometimes into the Cava above or below the Emulgent, but oftner into the Emulgent it self. The other, which goes down on the Right-hand, enters the Cava, commonly a little above the Emulgent, but very seldom is joined to the Emulgent it self.
